Sara Hashemi
Sara Hashemi

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A Viagra-like pill might slow cognitive decline in people with early Alzheimer’s disease, according to study results presented November 16 at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference.

The experimental treatment—a tablet called AR1001 developed by the South Korean company AriBio—is already sold in the drugmaker’s country as a medication for erectile dysfunction. Now, a year-long international study that enrolled more than 1,500 people with Alzheimer’s disease found it delayed the progression of cognitive decline in patients who weren’t taking other dementia treatments. However, the effect vanished when researchers examined the entire group taking the investigational drug.

Nevertheless, the findings “represent an important milestone in the development of new treatments for Alzheimer’s disease,” says Fred Kim , managing director of AriBio’s operations in the United States, to Lucia Auerbach at Inc .

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia, which affects about 57 million people worldwide. No cure currently exists for the neurodegenerative disease, although there are treatments that can help delay its progression and manage symptoms.

In the new clinical trial, called Polaris-AD , researchers enrolled patients with mild Alzheimer’s across 13 countries. They were randomized into groups that either took a daily dose of 30 milligrams of AR1001—less than a third of what people typically take for erectile dysfunction—or a placebo, Elie Dolgin reports for the Washington Post . The researchers examined the participants’ dementia progression with an assessment that scores cognitive and functional measures , including memory, problem-solving and ability to care for themselves, based on interviews with the patients and their caregivers.

Analyses revealed that at the year mark, the drug had slowed cognitive decline in the 604 participants not taking other dementia drugs by 31 percent compared with the placebo group. But when expanded to everyone in the experimental arm—including those taking donepezil or memantine for dementia—AR1001 failed to delay disease progression.

The most common adverse effects were diarrhea, falls and dizziness, according to Judy George at MedPage Today . These events led to around 5 percent of participants in the AR1001 group and 2 percent of participants in the placebo group dropping out of the trial.

The well-known erectile dysfunction medication was originally developed in the 1980s for the heart condition angina , chest pain that happens when less blood flows into the heart. However, later testing showed it wasn’t effective as an angina treatment.

Experts not involved in the study have welcomed the findings, though they are cautious. “It’s early days to say much definitively,” says Atticus Hainsworth , a neuroscientist at City St. George’s, University of London, who wasn’t involved in the trial but is evaluating AR1001 for another brain condition, to the Washington Post . Still, data from the subset where the drug appears to have helped “looks pretty good to me.”

So, how could a Viagra-like medication have a beneficial effect on cognitive decline? Researchers aren’t entirely sure, but it’s likely because erectile dysfunction drugs block an enzyme that breaks down a chemical messenger called cGMP, writes Rahul Sidhu , a neuroscientist at the University of Sheffield in England, for the Conversation .

This allows the messenger to accumulate, allowing blood vessels to relax. That helps with blood flow, which is how the medications alleviate erectile dysfunction. That same signal also works in the brain, where it helps nerve cells send information to one another. Scientists suspect that by boosting the amount of cGMP, those neurons can survive longer and continue to communicate.

The trial leaves the door open for further research. For instance, it’s unclear why AR1001 worked better for participants not already taking dementia medications. “We all have that question right now,” says Sharon Sha , a neurologist at Stanford University who led the trial, to the Washington Post .

Still, the results don’t mean people should start taking currently available erectile dysfunction medications for dementia.

“AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra,” says Richard Oakley , associate director of research and innovation at the Alzheimer’s Society, a nonprofit in the United Kingdom, in a statement . “But it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease.”

Catherine Lepage will have you leaping out of your desk chair with her self-directed “Dancing on Osees.” The irresistible animation features a quirky troupe of characters who can’t help but get down to “Together Tomorrow.” As the energetic track bolts forward, so do the hand-drawn dancers, who Lepage captures through stop-motion collages on paper.

The Montréal-based artist graciously shares glimpses behind the scenes on Instagram.

items.title: The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work
items.author: Annie Melchor
items.summary: Genetic information is sturdy, but its physical structure is sensitive. Natural tools for repairing a cell’s thousands of daily injuries are fundamental to gene-editing technologies. The post The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work first appeared on Quanta Magazine

images.caption: Lámina de Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Humans have debated the meaning of life for many millennia, but from evolution’s perspective, it is simple: Preserve the genome. Of course, mutation is allowed, as is the genetic mixing and matching of sexual reproduction, to create variety and evolutionary diversity. But we all exist because a viable lineage of DNA has persisted for 4 billion years. The genome’s policy is typically, “If the code works, don’t change it.”

You’d think, then, that cells would keep their DNA under lock and key, protected from the elements like the precious blueprint it is. But this isn’t possible. DNA is a working document. Cells need near-constant access to these instructions for making the molecules required by life. The huge, complex molecular structure is therefore exposed to nonstop assault by the by-products of everyday cellular metabolism, as well as environmental factors, such as radiation (including ultraviolet and X-ray), alcohol, pesticides, and more.

“DNA damage occurs all the time,” said Björn Schumacher , a molecular biologist at the University of Cologne. “[DNA] contains all the information for building a cell, building an organism, maintaining cells and tissues, and all that — but yet it is surprisingly unstable.”

He estimates that some cells endure up to 100,000 DNA damage events every day. “Damage to the DNA is the default,” he said. These events can injure sections of the DNA molecule — or, worse, break the strand in half. Even minor DNA damage risks changing or destroying the essential instructions a cell needs to operate, which can make cells malfunction, die, or become cancerous.

However, many of those tens of thousands of daily lesions get repaired quickly. Cells have native repair mechanisms that recognize and replace faulty DNA before lasting damage and dysfunction set in. In fact, the ability to repair damaged or broken DNA had to evolve at essentially the same time as DNA, Schumacher said, “because you cannot have stable genetic information without DNA repair.”

These mechanisms are essential not only to the evolutionary lineage of all known life, but also to promising technologies to treat genetic diseases. Scientists and doctors who experiment with gene editing must rely on DNA’s natural self-editing and repair tools to insert, delete, or mutate genes to study and treat disease.

So perhaps instead of a master blueprint protected behind glass, it’s better to imagine DNA as a beloved cookbook that is constantly in use. While it’s open on the kitchen counter, it’s bound to get splattered with sauce — or even have a page ripped. But spills can be wiped off. Torn pages can be taped up. And a smear obscuring an odd ingredient might even improve a recipe.

To understand how DNA gets damaged so easily, we need to see its structure, beyond the impossible elegance of the double helix. Most DNA is packed into chromosomes, dense structures formed by long, delicate filaments of DNA wrapped tightly around proteins. If you were to unwrap the DNA and untwist its double helix, you’d see a ladder made of nucleotides: the building blocks of DNA.

A single DNA strand — one side rail and half of each rung — encodes a specific arrangement of the four nucleotides, also known as bases. Each is a complex molecule represented by a single letter: A, T, G, or C. Across from it is a backup on the opposite, complementary strand, made up of each nucleotide’s natural partner (A’s partner is T, and G’s is C). The “rungs” of the DNA ladder are held together with relatively weak, transient bonds that allow the helix to be opened and closed like a zipper, so enzymes can access, read, and copy the code.

In 1994, Maria Jasin’s team first showed that intentionally introducing a double-strand break could compel DNA to repair the injury with an introduced gene sequence.

“[DNA has] all that clever structure to it, to enable it to come apart and replicate,” said Penny Jeggo , a molecular biologist who is now emeritus faculty at the University of Sussex. “But a consequence of [that structure] is that it’s sensitive to damage, and unlike proteins or RNA, it actually matters if it gets damaged.”

Even though DNA is precious, it also needs to be constantly accessed to provide the instructions for making the cells’ proteins. And it’s important to remember that the enzymes don’t “read” it from a distance. Every step is a tactile, chemical process. Like toddlers, enzymes physically touch, interact with, and occasionally change the DNA to work with it.

“[DNA is] a working molecule,” said Maria Jasin , a molecular biologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “So just by its nature, DNA is going to be subject to chemical forces that will modify it.”

items.title: These Endangered Snakes Are Some of the Most Beautiful in North America. Here's How Conservationists Are Trying to Save Them
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Fewer than 2,000 San Francisco garter snakes are estimated to live in their native home of two California counties. So, experts are raising some babies at the San Francisco Zoo to give them a head start before releasing the creatures into the wild

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
A man wearing a white t-shirt and a grey hat checking a bin

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Covered in vibrant blue, red and black stripes, the San Francisco garter snake is considered one of the most beautiful snakes in North America. But the nonvenomous species’ good looks have also made it a target for illegal collectors, and other threats—including habitat loss and invasive species—have further reduced its population. Fewer than 2,000 individuals are estimated to remain in two Northern California counties, and the species has been on the federal endangered species list since it was created in 1967.

Now, conservationists are hoping to give the population a boost by releasing 62 captive-raised young snakes into the wild. It’s the first time they’ve attempted such an effort, according to a November 10 announcement from the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens.

“This is an extraordinary accomplishment for everyone who has worked for generations to protect this remarkable species,” says Karine Tokatlian , a biologist with the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen), one of the organizations collaborating on the project, in the statement. “This first release is an important step toward building healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term.”

Planning for the project has been underway for at least a decade, reports the Washington Post ’s Kyle Melnick. But on-the-ground efforts kicked off last year, when biologists carefully captured ten pregnant females in a Midpen preserve and brought them to the San Francisco Zoo. There, the females gave birth to slender babies, which spent about a year growing and feeding on earthworms.

The mothers, meanwhile, were returned to the wild. “We tried to release them at the exact points we caught them,” Elliot Schoenig , a biologist with the U.S. Geological Survey’s Western Ecological Research Center, another project partner, told the San Francisco Chronicle ’s Kurtis Alexander last year. “For the most part, they just cruised back in. Some skirted the edges of the pond, which is their typical foraging behavior. Hopefully, they’ll encounter a frog and settle back in.”

Once the youngsters were about a foot long, experts conducted genetic testing and used the results to determine where best to release them. Roughly a third of the juveniles were returned to the area where their mothers lived, while the others were released in areas of San Mateo County that needed a population boost and greater genetic diversity. Conservationists are not revealing the specific locations over concerns that illegal collectors will seek them out.

“Even for a whole bunch of biologists who are typically not the most emotional people in their work, [the releases were] impactful,” Ariel Starr , a wildlife ecologist with Midpen, tells the Washington Post .

The Golden State hosts nearly 50 native species of snakes .

Scientists call this process head-starting, meaning they raise young animals in captivity when they’re considered the most vulnerable to threats like predation and competition for prey. Once they’re deemed large enough to tackle some of these challenges, the creatures are released into the wild. This technique is intended to boost the juveniles’ chances of survival, hopefully allowing them to reach sexual maturity and reproduce.

Zooming out, conservationists hope to one day get the species off the federal endangered list, which would mean establishing at least ten self-sustaining breeding populations with at least 200 snakes each. To do that, they’re also improving the snakes’ habitat, monitoring wild populations, educating the public and supporting populations of the threatened California red-legged frog , one of the snakes’ primary prey species.

“By protecting and restoring the landscapes that the San Francisco garter snake depends on, we’re also investing in the long-term health and resilience of the region’s environment,” Tokatlian tells KQED ’s Sarah Mohamad.

In the meantime, biologists have already captured a new round of pregnant females, which have birthed more than 130 babies at the zoo. If all goes as planned, they’ll be released into the wild next year.

The recent conservation efforts have given conservationists reason for optimism. But challenges remain.

“If we don’t have more snakes out there, they could disappear in our lifetime,” Rochelle Stiles , director of field conservation at the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens, told the San Francisco Chronicle .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
While researching the rising alarm over the impact of wildfires on babies in utero, I realized I was writing my own story

LOOKOUT: Smoke hovers over kids watching a wildfire burn across the border from Washington state into British Columbia in 2023.

New Year’s Eve 2019 on the far south coast of Australia was a day without dawn. At nine that morning, the sun was obscured by bushfire smoke rendering the land dizzyingly dark at the height of antipodean summer, like a midday solar eclipse. As one of the region’s obstetricians would painfully discover in the weeks that followed, the black morning skies turned out to be an augur of grievous climate consequences suffered by the unborn.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus . To get it in print, join by Nov 30 .

Photos from that Australian day show a hellish, red-tinted world: hundreds of people in bright summer attire evacuated to strips of beach typically postcard picture-perfect. But the photos fail to capture the heat, a 104 degrees Fahrenheit stew that barely cooled at night. Nor do they show the 62 mile-per-hour gale force winds that fanned flames into explosive thunderclouds, injecting smoke from burning gum trees 100,000 feet up into the stratosphere. There, the sun-warmed smoke generated a self-sustaining vortex five miles tall and 600 miles across with its own ozone hole, the likes of which atmospheric scientists had never before seen.

December 2019 had been abnormally dry and hot across Eastern Australia, especially in New South Wales, where temperatures ran almost 6 degrees F hotter than the monthly average. By New Year’s Eve, 100 fires raged across the region, most sparked by dry lightning. The flames grew explosively, triggering 38 firestorms over eastern Australia that grew with the ferocity of volcanic eruptions. Atmospheric scientists later dubbed the spate of fire-induced pyrocumulonimbus thunderstorms that erupted the “Australian New Year Super Outbreak.”

On the ground, conditions tightened, like a violin string ready to snap. There were more fires, bigger fires, faster fires. “They were coming from the north and coming up from the south, and there was this impending sense of threat,” said Michael Holland, the senior obstetrician in Moruya, a beach town four hours south of Sydney, with a population of about 4,300. With highways out of town cut off and no safe egress, thousands had to shelter in place. “Every park had camper vans, mobile homes, caravans,” Holland recalled. “There were people with goats and there were people with sheep. It was almost biblical: people evacuating, waiting for the ark to be built.”

Holland was in his 60s and a fixture of Moruya’s maternity ward, located in the town’s small general hospital. A ruddy-faced, quiet-spoken man who embodies the stoic character of his country, Holland quickly teamed up with an ER physician to set up triage at his hospital.

Moruya had lost power, and the hospital emergency generator barely had power to run an X-ray machine. Food and meds were spoiling in lukewarm fridges and stalled sewage pumps stagnated toilet bowls. Holland’s own home was under evacuation, so he and his family slept on the floor of his medical practice for five days. It felt like the apogee of a longer arc of misery as the Black Summer burned its way through the season. Smoke lingered in an ever-present ceiling all summer long. “For months we didn’t see the stars,” Holland said.

By mid-January, rain and cooler temperatures finally provided respite. In the following weeks, as smoke finally cleared from the skies, Holland discovered something that surprised and then shocked him. Three women in their third trimesters experienced “fetal death in utero,” or stillbirths.

In a typical year of practice, Holland saw about 350 births at the Moruya hospital, of which one might be a stillbirth, typically from prematurity or fetal abnormalities. In the recent cluster of three stillbirths, each of the placentas was highly abnormal. The tissue was thin, calcified, grainy to the touch. Typically, placentas resemble a pizza-shaped liver, all spongy and deep burgundy.

Although Holland didn’t know it at the time of the fires, in late 2019 a team of Belgian scientists had published a study that claimed, for the first time, to find evidence of black carbon particulates on the fetal side of the placenta. Later studies found particulates from air pollution in fetal cord blood, too, proof that the microscopic constituents of wildfire smoke can pollute not just a mother’s blood but her fetus’ too.

Public health experts now estimate that some 15,000 pregnant Australians and their fetuses were exposed to the Black Summer fires. While most were spared the brutal losses suffered by Holland’s patients, the smoke’s impact was measurable. Pregnant people are especially vulnerable to poor air quality since they breathe for two, taking in about 50 percent more air in their day to meet growing oxygen demands. One analysis of pregnant women found those exposed to the Black Summer fires in early- to mid-pregnancy were more likely to have their water break before 37 weeks, a leading cause of preterm birth. That same study found that the 2019 Black Summer bushfires were associated with an 11 percent higher risk of stillbirth, although the incidence was mercifully small enough as to preclude statistical significance.

Today, Holland is retired from his medical practice and is a member of the Australian parliament. He spoke to me about his work as an obstetrician with a natural buoyancy, describing how shortly after clamping the umbilical cord, the uterus, previously ballooned to cocoon the baby, deflates and loosens the placenta, which birth practitioners typically examine. This practice of midwives and obstetricians gathering round the placenta always conjured ancient history for him. “It reminds me of some fortune teller in ancient Rome looking at the entrails or something,” he said.

items.title: 20 Years of BHL. Help Us Keep Flying!
items.author: Nicole Kearney
items.summary: Last year, you gave BHL wings. This year, BHL turned 20! As we approach our first anniversary of independence, help us raise US$20,000 by 31 December to sustain BHL and keep biodiversity knowledge freely accessible to everyone, everywhere.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Last year, you gave BHL wings. This year, BHL turned 20. And on 31 December, we’ll complete our first full year of independent flight.

As this extraordinary year draws to a close, we’re inviting our global community to help us reach one final anniversary milestone: raise US$20,000 by 31 December to sustain BHL and support its future.

Bewick’s Swan ( Cygnus minor ), Pl. 10, from The Birds of Great Britain , Vol. 5 (1873), by John Gould. Illustration by Joseph Wolf and Henry Constantine Richter. View in BHL .

At the end of 2025, BHL faced the greatest challenge in its history . After nearly two decades of support from the Smithsonian Institution, we needed to establish a new, independent future.

Through our #GiveBHLWings campaign, supporters from around the world helped us raise more than US$50,000 in the final weeks of 2025. Alongside the extraordinary commitment of our consortium members and partners, that support helped BHL begin a new chapter on 1 January 2026.

We’ve secured all our existing staff positions , successfully relocated BHL’s servers and website infrastructure to the Field Museum , begun our Platform Modernization Project , welcomed new consortium members , and strengthened partnerships across our global community. Together, these achievements have laid the foundation for a stronger, more sustainable BHL.

And, of course, we’ve celebrated 20 years of making biodiversity knowledge freely accessible! Throughout the year, our BHL at 20 anniversary blog series has explored the remarkable collections, discoveries, people, and partnerships that have shaped BHL over the past two decades.

Today, more than 64 million pages of biodiversity literature remain freely available to everyone, everywhere, helping people around the world research, discover, and better understand the natural world.

BHL’s transition to independence was an extraordinary achievement. But keeping this global resource freely accessible requires ongoing investment in the people, technology, and infrastructure that make BHL possible. Your support will also help us improve the discoverability of our collections, strengthen connections with other biodiversity data resources, and make centuries of biodiversity knowledge more accessible and useful than ever before.

Last year, our community helped secure BHL’s future. Now, as we approach our first anniversary of independence, we’re asking you to help sustain it.

Our goal is to raise US$20,000 by 31 December , marking the close of BHL’s 20th anniversary year and helping sustain the critical work ahead.

Whether you’ve supported BHL for years or only recently discovered our collections, your donation will help keep biodiversity knowledge open and accessible to everyone, everywhere.

For other ways to support BHL, including major gifts and legacy giving, explore our Ways to Give page.

Needle-tailed Swift ( Acanthyllis caudacuta ), Pl. 2, from Coloured Figures of the Birds of the British Islands , Vol. 2 (1885–1897). Illustration by John Gerrard Keulemans. View in BHL .

items.title: Once Called Home by Lockkeepers and Park Rangers, This 200-Year-Old House Along the Historic Chesapeake and Ohio Canal Is Now Opening Its Doors to Overnight Guests
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: From the 1830s to the 1920s, Lockhouse 8 provided living quarters for the generations of lockkeepers who helped keep boats moving along canal, a critical route from the Atlantic Ocean to the American interior

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sarah Kuta
A man standing next to a mule near a boat in the water

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From the 1830s to the 1920s, Lockhouse 8 provided living quarters for the generations of lockkeepers who helped kept boats moving along the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal , which ran between Washington, D.C. and Cumberland, Maryland. Now, after undergoing renovations, the 196-year-old home is welcoming overnight guests, giving visitors to C&O Canal National Historical Park a unique way to experience the region’s history.

Lockhouse 8 is the newest addition to the Canal Quarters Program . Since 2007, the nonprofit C&O Canal Trust and the National Park Service have been partnering to breathe new life into many of the historic lockhouses located along the canal.

Lockhouse 22 became the first to welcome overnight guests, in 2010. Since then, the program has grown to eight lockhouses, each with its own time period and interpretive theme. Lockhouse 22, for instance, is set in the 1830s and ‘40s, during the early phases of canal construction, while Lockhouse 10 explores the New Deal era of the 1930s, when workers with the Civilian Conservation Corps repaired the canal.

“Staying overnight in a lockhouse provides a unique opportunity to immerse yourself in these stories,” Arden Shaer, associate director of the Canal Quarters Program, tells BBC Travel ’s Chelsey Stone.

Guests can reserve a lockhouse for up to three nights in a row, with nightly rates ranging from $75 to $175. The entire registration fee goes toward maintenance and restoration work, as well as educational experiences, so “when you stay here, you’re actually helping to preserve the house,” Tymber Compher, a spokeswoman for the C&O Canal Trust, tells WJLA ’s Adam Longo.

Each lockhouse can accommodate up to eight overnight guests, but visitors must supply their own linens. They have varying levels of amenities, with some offering modern niceties like indoor plumbing, while others have only outhouses.

“It’s a unique experience,” Compher tells WJLA. “It’s not like staying in an Airbnb or commercialized hotel.”

The canal’s history dates back more than 200 years. After the War of 1812 , the nation’s postwar priorities shifted to economic growth, westward expansion and improved transportation. One ambitious proposal called for the construction of a canal that would connect the Potomac River with the Ohio River Valley, creating a direct water route between the East Coast and the country’s growing western territories.

To bring the idea to life, Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania chartered the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal Company. Construction began on July 4, 1828, but the project proved far more challenging than anticipated, with difficult terrain, scarce building materials and a lack of large-scale contractors slowing progress.

On the same day that President John Quincy Adams broke ground on the canal, work started on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad . Its first stone was laid by Charles Carroll , the last surviving signer of the Declaration of Independence. The success of the railroad would eventually contribute to the canal's obsolescence.

When completed in 1850 , the 184.5-mile canal stretched from Georgetown in Washington, D.C., to Cumberland, Maryland, providing a vital transportation route for coal, lumber, agricultural products and other goods. (Funding issues, legal disputes and rough terrain prevented it from reaching the Ohio River.) Boats traveled through 74 locks that raised and lowered them through the canal’s 605-foot elevation change, while mules walking along the adjacent towpath pulled the vessels through the narrow waterway. Lockkeepers and their families lived in 57 lockhouses situated along the canal, often awakening as early as 2 a.m. “to the sound of the boatman’s horn or cry of ‘Hey-y-y-y lock,’” Stone writes for BBC Travel. Today, only 26 lockhouses remain.

The newly opened Lockhouse 8 is a 725-square-foot home located in the “ Seven Locks ” section of the park near Cabin John, Maryland, about ten miles from the heart of Washington, D.C. Over the years when the canal was in operation, Lockhouse 8 housed nine lockkeepers as they helped boats navigate the busy stretch near Georgetown. At the canal’s peak, that meant manning the eighth lock for more than 500 boats per day.

After the canal stopped operating in 1924 , the family of the last lockkeeper, Charles Spong, continued to live in Lockhouse 8 until the 1950s. And after President Dwight D. Eisenhower established the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Monument in 1961, it briefly housed a park ranger and his family. Then, Lockhouse 8 sat empty for decades.

From the early 2000s until 2019, it served as a nature center. It lay dormant again until 2025, when the C&O Canal Trust and National Park Service decided to rehabilitate it for the Canal Quarters Program.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.

Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.

Find out where AI progress is running into tougher challenges.

Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.

The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.

But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.

Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 AI may have cracked math’s greatest unsolved problem
Anthropic’s Claude was used to prove the Riemann hypothesis. (WSJ $)
+ Two groups have independently verified the proof. (Guardian)
+ It could be the biggest math breakthrough in decades. (New Scientist $)
+ AI may be changing who gets to do math. (MIT Technology Review)

2 The COP31 climate talks have collapsed after a fossil fuels row
The EU rejected a deal it called “greenwashing.” (NBC News)
+ Saudi Arabia, Russia, and India opposed mentioning fossil fuels. (BBC)
+ Calls are growing for “net negative” instead of just net zero. (Nature)
+ Last year’s talks avoided fossil fuels. (MIT Technology Review)

3 The woman at the center of Nvidia’s scandal has ties to China’s military
Firms in her family’s network work with Chinese defense contractors. (NYT $)
+ Her associate allegedly ran the chip smuggling behind the scenes. (WSJ $)
+ US intelligence says she was in touch with a Chinese spy official. (ABC)
+ Republicans are pushing a new AI strategy to counter Beijing. (Reuters $)

4 Hackers have breached the FBI’s criminal information database
It contains information used by law enforcement at all levels. (AP)
+ Hackers also breached an Agriculture Department system. (NBC News)
+ And the Austrian foreign ministry’s website. (Reuters $)

5 Russia, the US, and Israel have stalled global rules on “killer robots”
The UK, Japan, South Korea, and Turkey also resisted binding rules. (Politico)
+ Around 100 nations backed regulations, but arms producers balked. (CNBC)
+ Talks will continue through 2028. (AP)

6 Trump says he’ll ban US companies from building data centers abroad
He threatened them with a “tremendous tax.” (CNBC)
+ Electricity is fuelling the data center backlash. (MIT Technology Review)

7 US lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars
They plan to prohibit sales of Chinese vehicles in the US. (Quartz)

8 Trump’s visa crackdown has pushed tech workers to leave the US
It’s driving engineers and researchers overseas. (Bloomberg $)

9 GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could free up farmland larger than Italy
Their use could transform the global food system. (Conversation)
+ They may also slow biological aging. (MIT Technology Review)

10 BepiColombo has become the second spacecraft to orbit Mercury
Its probes will study the planet’s surface and surroundings. (Nature)
+ Mercury’s ancient ice could hold clues to the origins of life. (New Yorker $)

“It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.”

—John Kennedy, US senator from Louisiana, tells NBC’s Meet the Press that Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could prove costly for efforts to prevent China from obtaining AI chips.


On the ground in Ukraine’s largest Starlink repair shop

Starlink is critical to Ukraine’s fight against Russia, but Donald Trump’s fickle foreign policy and reports of Elon Musk restricting Ukraine’s access to the service have cast the technology’s future in the country into doubt.

For now, Starlink access largely comes down to the unofficial community of users and engineers, including the expert “Dr. Starlink”—famous for his creative ways of customizing the systems—who have kept Ukraine in the fight, both on and off the front line.

He gave MIT Technology Review exclusive access to his unofficial Starlink repair workshop in the city of Lviv. Here’s what we learned.

We can still have nice things

items.author: Leonard David
items.summary: A nearly 50-year-old treaty dictates international and commercial collaboration in space, but space law may need updating in the face of growing cosmic capitalism The post Is the Privatization of Space Sustainable? appeared first on Nautilus .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A nearly 50-year-old treaty dictates international and commercial collaboration in space, but space law may need updating in the face of growing cosmic capitalism

Gone are the days when hurling payloads into space was a purely governmental effort. There is an ever-growing constellation of private startups engaged in a final frontier make over.

The privatization of space is truly on the move. News of the latest SpaceX launch of its Starship and successful return-to-launch pad recovery as well as other private space sector achievements are becoming near-daily events.

Low Earth orbit is already crowded with commercial satellites, and the vision of what’s to come includes commercial space stations, networks of floating data centers, constellations of power-beaming satellites, made-in-space pharmaceutical factories, gas-and-go refueling facilities, even rubbernecking space tourists in search of the most exotic of destinations.

But as we blast off into this uncertain future, what laws, international agreements, or treaties might guardrail the development? Are we rushing headlong into conflict? Or are we floating peacefully into a shared and harmonious collaboration in the heavens?

Some futuristic forecasters see space as an evolving economic zone that may one day span the distance between Earth and the moon.

Amazon founder and space capitalist, Jeff Bezos, is projecting that millions of people will dwell in the vacuum of space in just two decades time. Indeed, that shift could occur much faster than many foresee, buoyed by governmental investments in exploring and exploiting the cosmos and powered by a potent mix of advances in artificial intelligence and robotics. Will this result in a Wild West of private space ventures?

Matt Weinzierl, professor of business administration at the Harvard Business School and co-author of Space to Grow: Unlocking the Final Economic Frontier , says that “privatization” is not really the right term for what’s happening. “The government is not getting out of space. In fact, the government is still an absolutely central player,” he says. “I call it ‘commercialization,’ because the big change is the rise of market forces in space.”

Indeed, the infusion of private capital has already changed the complexion of humanity’s incursions into space. In October, the Office of Space Commerce—an arm of the United States Department of Commerce—and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released a report titled, “Building an In-Space Circular Economy.”

That report centers on the fact that, “traditional space activities have followed a linear, single mission model in which spacecraft are designed, launched, operated, and ultimately disposed of through atmospheric reentry or relocation to graveyard orbits.” Thanks to the growth of the commercial space sector, this “take-make-use-dispose” paradigm is increasingly challenged by the economic and operational realities of long-duration space activity.

A “circular space economy” is an alternate approach, underscores the report, that could reduce dependence on terrestrial resupply by extending the lifetimes of assets in space through the inspection, servicing, repair, reuse, repurposing, and recycling of space systems.

Casting an eye to the future, the report says that building an in-space circular economy will require coordination among policy, finance, technology, and standards organizations. That’s prelude to a functioning circular space economy that depends on a persistent physical and digital infrastructure. “Servicing hubs, modular platforms, transportation networks, manufacturing and recycling facilities, power generation, and communications must operate as parts of an interconnected system,” states the report.

A long-time witness to the evolution of low Earth orbit from a barren frontier into an emerging marketplace is Jeffrey Manber, a special representative to the chairman and CEO at Voyager Technologies, a defense technology and space solutions company. “Even at this early stage in commercial development, low Earth orbit services are fulfilling critical national security needs and, at the same time, acting as a foundation for emerging markets,” he says.

Manber says he’s confident that in 10 years, low Earth orbit will be far more populated with services and platforms than today. Commercial space markets, he adds, take decades to develop and reach emerging status, and only after governments make the initial commitment to invest in such frontiers. In his view, there will be a number of orbiting space stations in different inclinations, owned by different organizations and companies focused on different markets, with some focused on in-space research and manufacturing. Others will be hotels, warehouses, and fuel depots, some U.S.-owned while others are supported by other nations.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From finding human figures in the stars to creating prehistoric cave art, we’ve been anthropomorphising our world for millennia. Now, machine-learning technologies can generate photorealistic images, synthetic voices that laugh and pause for breath, and chatbots that crush the Turing test. We’re seeing the first generation in history for whom the line between humans and their representations could all but vanish.

In this video essay for the digital publication Fully Human, the UK animator and filmmaker Lewis Heriz interrogates where this is taking us. We inevitably build our world through symbols, he says, but the hall-of-mirrors reality we’re rapidly creating may be leading us down a perilous path. However, he argues, we’re not without agency. Instead of submitting to a world where data and people are indistinguishable, we should be thinking critically and imaginatively about how we might use AI in ways that preserve our humanity.

Artificial ‘creativity’ is unstoppable. Grappling with its ethics is up to us

Why we should worry less about ‘sentient’ AIs and more about what we’re teaching them

AI isn’t merely bad at writing. It does not and cannot write

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Massive clouds of dust roll into Melbourne on 8 February 1983 as a consequence of droughts induced by the extreme El Niño of 1982-83. Photo by Trevor Farrar/Australian Bureau of Meteorology

is associate professor of environmental history at Georgetown University and was the 2024/25 Blumberg NASA/Library of Congress Chair in Astrobiology, Exploration, and Scientific Innovation. His latest book is Ripples on the Cosmic Ocean: An Environmental History of Our Place in the Solar System (2025) . He lives in Washington, DC.

As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

It’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

Global sea-surface temperature anomalies in November 2015, at the peak of the 2014-16 El Niño event, one of the strongest recorded by meteorological instruments. Courtesy NOAA

I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

The past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño ’s future on a warming planet.

A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

It’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño , meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century . Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.

When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).

El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific

Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.

“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”

“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

Tempered expectations

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

items.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
items.author: Ananya Bhattacharya
items.summary: Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

images.caption: Lámina de Rest of World

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.

Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document.

“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World . “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.

For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World . It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.

Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.

Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.

“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World . “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”

For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World .

Moving a position can mean uprooting a family.” George Carrillo, CEO of and staffing company HireMe

“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.

Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.

“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World . “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Days before the Venice Biennale opened, the Golden Lion jury resigned amid calls to exclude Israel from the festival. Dozens of artists and pavilions took themselves out of the running in solidarity. Now, as the exhibition draws to a close, the Biennale is ready to present its visitors’ choice awards — a “poisoned chalice,” in the words of the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA), that “few want to win.” ANGA reflects on a historic year of organizing against attempts to artwash Israel’s assault on Palestine in an opinion piece today.

As gamers everywhere pore over Grand Theft Auto VI, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia sits down with Miami-based artists misael soto and Leo Castañeda to make sense of the game’s many tensions and complexities, while Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar tracks down its various art references. In another form of uncanny valley, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle wanders through empty corporate offices in Midtown Manhattan, transformed by artists who dismantle the systems of technocracy from the inside out. More to start your week below.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

The Venice Biennale’s Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide

Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. | Art Not Genocide Alliance

“Mighty Miniatures” Features Over 300 Tiny Artworks From Indigenous Communities Across the Western Hemisphere

Opening November 21 at the National Museum of the American Indian in New York, this exhibition includes masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries.

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time. | Valentina Di Liscia

  • From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.
  • Twenty artists and designers across the Americas will be featured in Malvestir at MoMA PS1 this spring, probing the historical and contemporary resonances of Latin American dress.

Fall 2026 Art and Architecture Books from Yale University Press

The Bayeux tapestry, a new biography of Edward Hopper, The Met’s exhibition catalogue on Krasner and Pollock, what architecture is, and more

Threading the Names of Alabama’s Black Belt History

In a community center across from Mt. Willing Baptist Church, a group of women is sewing the legacies of enslaved people into their quilts. | Carly Mattox

In a Midtown Office, Artists Sift Through the Junkspace of Capitalism

An intergenerational group of artists confronts technology as both a pathogen and a cure for today’s cultural ailments in the husk of an office at 260 Madison. | Phillip Pyle

So You Want to Run an Artist’s Estate?

A how-to guide on all things inventory, planning, appraisals, conservation, and more. | John Seed

A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao

“I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”

  • A deep-dive into the fraught history of the Irish selkie, whose folklore is far more complicated and painful than its mainstream iterations would have us believe. [Aeon] 
  • The Jacobin is back with another bad take, this time via a senior editor who penned an opinion for the New York Times lambasting “Woke 1.0.” Alec Karakatsanis breaks down the strawman argument. [X]
  • Devotees of Fiona, the viral beloved hippo who died last week, are flocking to the Cincinnati Zoo to share tributes to the gentle giant. [Guardian]

Eadweard Muybridge and the Making of the Motion Picture

items.title: Inside Edward Said’s World
items.author: Hyperallergic
items.summary: A new film about the Palestinian thinker, reviewed by a former students of his, and when does a documentary become an art performance?

Inside Edward Said’s World
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight. 

The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one?

And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.

—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

Celebrate Indigenous Cinema and Storytelling with Free Films

Available for only two weeks, this curated selection of 14 Indigenous films features stories of resilience, inspiration, and hope.

Hell Takes the Form of State Repression in 1971’s “The Devils”

Ken Russell’s film designed by Derek Jarman, newly released in a 4K restoration, mirrors the horrors unfolding outside our windows. | Phillip Pyle

Sara Flores Paints What the World Stands to Lose

“Every opportunity to show my work is a platform to raise attention on the struggle for self-determination and cultural resistance of the Shipibo people,” the artist told Hyperallergic.

The Ongoing Experiment of Millennium Film Workshop

Celebrating 60 years, the avant-garde space remains a supportive home for a community of experimental and non-commercial filmmakers. | Irene Lee

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

As a new documentary shows, the Palestinian scholar believed an intellectual must always oppose domination while cultivating resistance. | Moustafa Bayoumi

“The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn

Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s New York amid the HIV/AIDS crisis. | Eileen G’Sell

Piecing Together Romare Bearden’s Life

The best part of the new documentary about the famed artist is watching people interact with his work. | Dan Schindel

What Does Frida Kahlo Mean Today?

A new documentary poses this question across socio-cultural contexts, steering clear of whitewashing the artist’s personal history. | Eileen G’Sell

To Be Alone With Your Thoughts in ’70s New York

Fred Camper’s contemplative film “Suicide Note” was born out of grief and a city in collapse. | Dan Schindel

items.author: Colin Marshall

items.cleanReaderHtml:
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch, Girl with a Pearl Earring, and The Garden of Earthly Delights. But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece, also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece, seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The Aristotelian notion of “man” as a “rational animal” has seen its share of detractors, from the Cynics to Bertrand Russell to nearly the whole of Poststructuralist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to compress the debate between intellect and passion into a pithy aphorism: “Man is a rational animal who always loses his temper when he is called upon to act in accordance with the dictates of reason.”

We no longer need clever verbal barbs to refute too-optimistic assessments of human behavior. Economics is catching up: we have the language of neuroscience and psychology, which consistently tells us that humans decidedly do not behave rationally very often, but are driven by bias and biology in inexplicable ways. And for over a hundred years now, we’ve known that the clockwork Newtonian view of the physical universe turns out to be a much messier and indeterminate affair, as does the universe of the human mind.

Why, then, has so much economic theory operated with a kind of dogged Aristotelianism, insisting that the units of capitalist society, the workers, managers, investors, consumers, owners, renters, speculators, etc. behave in predictable ways? We have case after case showing that intelligence and critical reasoning often have little to do with success or failure in the market. In such cases, however, one often hears the “madness of crowds” or other clichés invoked as an explanation.

To illustrate, market reporters and business writers have seized upon the story of Isaac Newton’s spectacular rise and fall in the so-called “South Sea Bubble” of 1720. We find the story in Benjamin Graham’s 1949 classic The Intelligent Investor, a widely-read book that attributes the irrationality of market systems to an anthropomorphic entity named “Mr. Market.”

Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac Newton owned shares in the South Sea Company, the hottest stock in England. Sensing that the market was getting out of hand, the great physicist muttered that he ‘could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of the people.’ Newton dumped his South Sea shares, pocketing a 100% profit totaling £7,000. But just months later, swept up in the wild enthusiasm of the market, Newton jumped back in at a much higher price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 million in [2002–2003’s] money. For the rest of his life, he forbade anyone to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his presence.

The quotation in bold may or may not have been uttered by Newton, but the events Graham describes did indeed happen. As the Wall Street Journal’s Jason Zweig relates, University of Minnesota professor Andrew Odlyzko found that “Newton had shifted from a prudent investor with his money spread across several securities to a speculator who had plunged essentially all of his capital into a single stock. The great scientist was chasing hot performance as desperately as a day trader in 1999 or many bitcoin buyers in 2017.” (Odlyzko estimates Newton’s losses at closer to $4 million.) Perhaps it was not a metaphorical “Mr. Market” who cost Newton up to 77% “on his worst purchases,” nor was it widespread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass movement of passion that Enlightenment philosophers so feared.

Perhaps it was Newton himself who, Elena Holodny writes at Business Insider, “let his emotions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irrationality of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accurate to say Newton succumbed to greed when the bubble expanded. “Throughout history,” Barbara Kollmeyer writes at Market Watch in her interview with author Richard Dale, “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible participants in financial bubbles. And Sir Isaac Newton was only human, after all.” (How many at the top rung of society fell prey to Bernie Madoff’s schemes? And a century before the South Sea Bubble, hundreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the Dutch Tulip Bulb craze.)

Some business writers, like investment editor Richard Evans at The Telegraph, recommend a calculable formula to avoid losing a fortune in bubbles, advice that takes rational agency for granted. Perhaps it should not. In addition to citing the contagion of crowds, nearly every discussion of Newton’s folly allows that a failure of emotional discipline played a significant role. Benjamin Graham invokes another Aristotelian notion—the idea that “character” counts as much or more than intelligence when it comes to investing. “The investor’s chief problem,” he writes, “and even his worst enemy—is likely to be himself.”

Far fewer commenters note that the South Sea venture was itself a failure of character from its inception. The company had secured an exclusive monopoly on trade with South America; much of that trade involved selling slaves. It is also the case that the company artificially inflated its stock prices, and colluded with several MPs in insider trading schemes. The so-called “Bubble Act” of Parliament in 1720, presumably passed to prevent crashes like the one that devastated Newton, turned out to be a corporate giveaway. The terms of the act had been dictated by the South Sea Company in order to prevent other companies from poaching their investors. Although these circumstances are well-known to economic historians, they rarely make their way into commentary on Newton’s great loss.

Economists instead tend to blame abstractions for economic events like the South Sea Bubble, or they blame the overreaching profit-seeking of investors, and maybe for good reason. The other explanations haunt the margins: the inherently exploitative nature of most forms of corporate capitalism, and the corruption and collusion between the state and private enterprise that inhibits fair competition and makes it impossible for investors to evaluate the situation transparently. For all of his scientific and mathematical genius, Isaac Newton was no exception—he was just as subject to irrational greed as the next investor, and to the predatory machinations of “market forces.”

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

items.cleanReaderHtml: Costó 750.000 dólares (674.000 euros) pero ha recaudado más de 500 millones (448 millones de euros) en taquilla. Nikki, su protagonista, ha dado tanto repelús que la desconocida actriz que la interpretaba, Inde Navarrette, se ha infiltrado en las quinielas de las nominaciones de los próximos Oscar. La desquiciada enamorada de la película de terror Obsession es la chica de moda. Acaba de presentar el mítico Saturday Night Live y será Pícara en la nueva entrega de X-Men. Y todo por una interpretación asfixiante de una joven que, fruto de un hechizo, se convierte en la persona que más quiere en el mundo a Bear, su amigo de la infancia. En Variety dicen que las “expresiones inquietantes” y el “aire maníaco” de Navarrette son dignos de estatuilla. De su habilidad para revolver al espectador no hay duda, pero la película de Curry Barker ha abierto un debate enfrentado entre fans y especialistas del género: ¿es Obsession el paradigma del nuevo terror incel, una fábula sobre el privilegio masculino en el romance heterosexual, o es una película para el disfrute misógino del desmorone femenino?

items.summary: El rockismo es una enfermedad infantil. Y el premio por superarlo es la apertura a infinitas posibilidades

items.cleanReaderHtml: Para los que comenzamos temprano en los asuntos del pop y el rock, el objeto del deseo era sencillo: la buena música. Sencillo… y casi inaprensible. Las revistas musicales españolas, con la excepción de Fonorama, no se interesaban por la historia, las raíces de esos géneros; tampoco existía lo que podíamos llamar Crítica, con mayúscula. Las emisoras de FM eran, fuera de las capitales, más un rumor que una realidad y, de todos modos, no se podían pillar en muchos de los receptores. Entre los soportes, el formato dominante era el Extended Play, el disco de vinilo de 17 centímetros de diámetro, con cuatro canciones. Se consideraba que aquí apenas había mercado para su majestad el Long Play, con sus 30 centímetros; de hecho, fuera de Beatles y Stones, salían pocos LP encuadrables en la entonces llamada “música moderna”.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
New species can be discovered in all sorts of ways . In the case of Rhacophorus kurniatia , a type of Asian flying frog that’s only just been identified, it involved a trek deep into the Mekongga Mountains in Indonesia, to a secluded lake where thousands of frogs had congregated.

“We were moving up the mountain, and we came across this big pond covered in these green frogs,” Alan Hitch, one of the authors of a new study about Rhacophorus kurniatia , explained in a statement . “They were all over. You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special.”

They were quickly identified as being flying frogs, from the Rhacophorus genus. The large webbed feet, for gliding between trees, were the main giveaway. Further analysis revealed something not seen in other Rhacophorus species, though: The frogs deposit their eggs in gelatinous masses hanging above or near water, rather than in the typical foamy nests.

Distinctive, pointed snouts, as well as differences in the calls made by the frogs, confirmed that this was a species that hadn’t been observed and documented before.

“The team looked at hundreds and hundreds of specimens of frogs to describe the new species,” study author Andrew Engilis Jr. said in a statement . “Sometimes species can look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different—these are called cryptic species. This frog is an example of that. It looks very similar to other Rhacophorus , but its genetics and behavior show that it’s very distinctive.”

The identification of R. kurniatia is the culmination of four years of work on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is close to Borneo. Expeditions carried out by the researchers led them from sea level to the highest mountain peaks—with the new flying frog species discovered some 6,100 feet above sea level.

And there’s a bittersweet reason for the naming: The flying frog’s scientific name was chosen as a mark of respect for renowned herpetologist Hellen Kurniati, who died in 2024. She was one of the leading researchers studying amphibians and reptiles in Indonesia. She also helped to discover the new species that now shares her name.

Lead Image: Wahyu Trilaksono / Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .
