items.cleanReaderHtml:
Un estudio liderado por una investigadora de Exactas UBA analizó el impacto del glifosato que llega a lagunas y arroyos de la llanura pampeana sobre la reproducción y el desarrollo del pejerrey, revelando efectos diferenciales entre el principio activo y el producto formulado, que presenta altísimas tasas de mortalidad en larvas en las concentraciones más elevadas.

Las miles de toneladas de herbicidas que se aplican cada año sobre los campos de la llanura pampeana no sólo mejoran el rendimiento de las cosechas de soja, trigo, maíz y otros cereales y oleaginosas, al evitar que las malezas compitan con estos cultivos. También generan importantes daños a la salud y al medio ambiente: contaminan los cuerpos de agua adonde indefectiblemente llega buena parte de ese arsenal químico, afectando a “organismos no blanco”, por ejemplo, los peces.

En este marco, un estudio liderado por una investigadora de Exactas UBA analizó el impacto del glifosato sobre la reproducción y el desarrollo del pejerrey ( Odontesthes bonariensis ), una especie de agua dulce nativa de la Argentina, revelando diferentes efectos, dependiendo del compuesto –el principio activo del glifosato o bien el producto formulado– y de la etapa de desarrollo analizada.

Renata Menéndez Helman, investigadora del Laboratorio de Enzimología, Estrés Oxidativo y Metabolismo que funciona en el Instituto de Química Biológica de la Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales (IQUIBICEN, UBA-CONICET), trabaja desde hace años en la ecotoxicología del glifosato, el herbicida más utilizado en la Argentina y también a nivel global. Explica que desde la aprobación de los organismos genéticamente modificados resistentes a plaguicidas, la aplicación de agroquímicos en el país pasó de 38 mil toneladas anuales a más de 200 mil, de las cuales aproximadamente 150 mil toneladas corresponden al glifosato.

A pesar de que el glifosato no tiene una vida media muy larga en los cuerpos de agua, se aplica en forma tan masiva que hoy en día se lo considera un contaminante pseudopersistente.

“A punto tal que, a pesar de que el glifosato, por su estructura, no tiene una vida media muy larga en los cuerpos de agua, se aplica con una frecuencia tan alta y en forma tan masiva que hoy en día se lo considera un contaminante pseudopersistente. El tiempo que demanda el glifosato para ser removido por procesos naturales, su tasa de atenuación, no alcanza para mitigar la tasa de ingreso en los cuerpos de agua”, puntualiza.

El objetivo del estudio fue investigar los efectos de la exposición al glifosato sobre la calidad espermática, el éxito de la fecundación y el desarrollo embrionario y larvario del pejerrey, “un pez nativo, muy relevante desde el punto de vista ecológico pero también desde el comercial, en la pesca artesanal, deportiva, y también por su potencial uso en acuicultura”, señala Menéndez Helman. De ahí la pertinencia de analizar los efectos que provoca en estos peces la presencia de glifosato en lagunas y arroyos.

Facundo Rovera, Renata Menéndez y Emilia Colombo Fotografía: Luiza Cavalcante.

“Estudiar esos efectos específicamente en la reproducción y en el desarrollo nos permite hacer un abordaje sistémico del contaminante, porque durante el desarrollo se dan una gran cantidad de procesos y hay distintas ventanas de susceptibilidad. Entonces, se evalúan diversos efectos que se van integrando, desde lo bioquímico, desde lo celular, al nivel de los tejidos y de los órganos. Además, un efecto que se verifica en la fase reproductiva y en el desarrollo puede tener implicancias en términos poblacionales”.

El principal período de desove del pejerrey, entre septiembre y diciembre, coincide con meses en los que se produce una aplicación masiva de glifosato en los campos de cultivo.

El trabajo –publicado en Environmental Science and Pollution Research – analizó los efectos tóxicos del glifosato, tanto los de su principio activo como los de los productos formulados. “Ocurre que en muchos de estos productos fitosanitarios, al principio activo se le agregan coadyuvantes, compuestos que facilitan la absorción en la planta, potenciando su eficacia –advierte Menéndez Helman–. Estos compuestos pueden ser incluso más tóxicos y causar mayores efectos que el propio principio activo. En nuestro estudio, se observa una mortalidad de las larvas del ciento por ciento en pocas horas con la máxima concentración del formulado. ¿Esto significa que el efecto letal lo causa el coadyuvante? No lo sabemos, puede deberse a los coadyuvantes o a la interacción entre estos y el glifosato como principio activo. Como no hay obligación de declararlos en las etiquetas, no sabemos qué compuestos son y no podemos evaluar su efecto en forma independiente”.

El pejerrey es un pez nativo, muy relevante desde el punto de vista ecológico pero también desde el comercial, en la pesca artesanal, deportiva, y también por su potencial uso en acuicultura.

El efecto inicial analizado fue el de la motilidad espermática, es decir, la capacidad de desplazamiento de los espermatozoides. Los estudios revelaron, con la concentración más alta del producto formulado, un aumento estadísticamente significativo en la motilidad. Por el contrario, la exposición al principio activo provocó una disminución en los parámetros de motilidad espermática.

Menéndez Helman relativiza ese aparente efecto positivo del producto formulado. “Estos peces –explica– tienen fecundación externa: los espermatozoides y los oocitos deben encontrarse y fecundarse en el medio externo donde están presentes todos estos contaminantes. Pero además, estos espermatozoides son mótiles durante un tiempo muy breve, no mucho más de un minuto. Después dejan de moverse: la ventana que tienen para la fecundación es muy corta. Entonces, si bien inicialmente vemos, en los primeros diez segundos, un aumento de la motilidad espermática, esto en absoluto determina per se un mayor éxito reproductivo. Podría ocurrir que se produzca un agotamiento prematuro, que la disponibilidad de energía se consuma antes. Es una hipótesis que nos interesa evaluar: si el contaminante reduce el tiempo disponible para la fecundación”.

items.title: A Cult Grew Around the First Emperor of Rome in 27 B.C. A New Book Argues His Followers Might Have Created the Template for Christianity
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: Augustus was seen as a descendant of the gods who would go on to redefine authority. New research posits that his rule paved the way for Jesus

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Arts & Culture

Cover image of the Smithsonian Magazine November 2026 issue

items.cleanReaderHtml:
How did the scattered followers of an itinerant preacher come to form the most populous religion in the world? Tim Whitmarsh—a classicist at the University of Cambridge and author of magisterial books about empire, the early novel and more—offers a compelling answer in his new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity. To wit, Christianity took much of its shape from the cult of Augustus, first emperor of Rome.

The Augustan age saw a unique revolution that redefined authority, space and literature, remaking both the inner world and the outer. Augustus drew on centuries-old Roman prophecies to cast himself as the promised one . According to his propaganda, Italy experienced auguries and miracles at Augustus’ nativity; Augustus was declared a descendant of Rome’s mythical founder, Aeneas, and therefore of the gods, and he promised to renew Roman liberty from the decadence of the late Republic. As Whitmarsh writes: “The new world was presented as the fulfillment of all the best ideals of the old.” Just so, Jesus’s birth was claimed as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies about a coming emissary of God on Earth, and this novel form of monotheism was simultaneously cast as the fruition of the Hebrew faith.

Whitmarsh goes further, arguing: “What we call messianism is a symbolic byproduct of the concentration of absolute power over vast territories and multiple populations in the hands of one individual or family.” Jesus, then, is “the divine doppelgänger of the most powerful human authority imaginable,” i.e., Augustus, and Christianity came to operate “as a strange doppelgänger of the Roman imperial system.”

Just as unitary empire helped prepare people for the concept of a unitary god, Augustan infrastructure—including an empire-spanning network of roads—literally paved the way for the transmission of stories about Jesus and his followers. Letters and trade flourished, and religions, which had long been deeply tied to location, could become universal.

Whitmarsh has a keen eye for the religio-cultural give-and-take between Judea and Rome: “The Christian idea of a savior king ... is partially shaped by the prior model of Augustus as a world savior. But that model was itself partially indebted to Jewish messianic traditions.” Causality, after all, is a subtle thing, and Whitmarsh avoids oversimplifications. He invokes a cultural dynamic that he calls a “swirl,” which gets kicked up by political or technological revolution—but also precedes the revolution. It can be a hazy concept. But with Whitmarsh’s sharp and often inspired readings of history and literature, it offers an imprecise but necessary honesty. Thou shalt not bear false witness, indeed.

Augustus relied on poets like Virgil, the famed bard of the early Roman Empire, to popularize his reign.

Virgil’s eclogues, a series of 10 pastoral poems, describe a savior child born to a virgin mother. The poem is dated to 40 B.C.E. and has been interpreted by some as a prophecy of Christ.

Virgil wrote that the Earth would celebrate the savior’s birth with miracles: Snakes would die, and goats would no longer fear lions.

The poem’s vision is referred to as the Cumaean Prophecy—and itself may have been inspired by earlier sources, possibly the eastern cult of Mithras, or from the book of Isaiah.

Tim Whitmarsh draws parallels that suggest the Roman Empire may have helped shape Christianity

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

items.title: How Astronomers and Art Historians Are Working Together to Identify the Inspiration Behind Famous Works of Art
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: Researchers study paintings and literature to uncover untold history of the works, sometimes finding themselves trying to discern celestial bodies from dust

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Arts & Culture
The Evening Star
Cover image of the Smithsonian Magazine November 2026 issue
Prof. Don Olson
Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise
Friedrich

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the spring of 2025, I fell into some art detective work. My mission was to go to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and get close to The Evening Star by the German Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich . The Evening Star —a nickname for Venus —joined several works not previously displayed in the United States, part of a Friedrich exhibition called “The Soul of Nature,” honoring the 250th anniversary of the artist’s birth. According to the museum’s description, Venus could be seen as “a tiny bright dot” barely visible above a cloud bank. In the painting, three figures stand on a hill outside Dresden, Germany, at sunset. A young boy at center, his back to the viewer, lifts his arms in exultation. But where was the star? The work’s title character seemed to be missing from prints and art books depicting The Evening Star.

As a caver, I’m normally trying to solve mysteries deep in the earth. This unaccustomed aboveground task came to me, indirectly, from Don Olson , the astronomer and astrophysicist. In 2024, I’d casually met one of his research collaborators, Ava Pope , through her partner, Mike Newsome, both fellow caving enthusiasts. (The two often sponsored caver gatherings at their Virginia farm.) When Pope saw on social media that my wife, Kathy, and I were in New York for the weekend, she texted me. The exhibition would end in less than two months, and she explained that if I could find and photograph Venus, my images might help Olson unravel several mysteries: From what physical spot did Friedrich observe the scene? On what date? And who, for that matter, is the family depicted in the scene? I was determined to find out.

As I would learn, Olson and his students and collaborators have taken on a singular approach, finding new truths in paintings we thought we knew.

Olson began using astronomy to investigate creative works in the 1980s at Texas State University, when an English professor asked him for help understanding complex astronomical passages in “The Franklin’s Tale,” one of Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales . His astronomical research connected an abnormally high tide on the coast of Brittany—a major plot device in the story—to an extreme flood on December 19, 1340, which may have inspired the incident in Chaucer. Besides co-writing a paper about the various lines of evidence that led him to that date, Olson studied astronomical elements in a variety of other works: Claude Monet’s The Cliff, Étretat, Sunset (pinpointing the beach location where the artist stood); Vincent van Gogh’s White House at Night (the golden disk in the sky must be Venus around a sunset in June 1890, as opposed to sunrise, moonrise or moonset); Ansel Adams’ Autumn Moon (the remote and never-before-identified Yosemite location from which the photograph must have been taken); William Shakespeare’s Hamlet (whether the star in the opening scene is a planet, or Tycho’s supernova , or something else); Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (verifying that the “waking dream” she later described as inspiring her story happened on a moonlit evening in Switzerland on June 16, 1816); and historical events from ancient Rome (locating Julius Caesar’s first invasion of Britain ) to World War II (explaining a disastrous tide for Marines landing at Tarawa in the Central Pacific). Olson realized that many dates and locations where artworks were made, even the very scenes they depicted, had been incorrectly reported in books and exhibitions, which often gave conflicting years and places. Olson felt certain these were errors he could fix by combining astronomical data with site visits and deep dives into historical records.

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

A lanky figure who often wears blue jeans and a Texas State shirt, Olson has long softened his exacting attention to detail with lectures that feature such examples, to make science less “terrifying” to his students. In basic physics classes, he has cast rainbows across the room to explain refraction; in honors-program classes, he has taken undergraduates to Yosemite, Switzerland and other far-flung locations, immersing them in unforgettable fieldwork.

In 2008, Pope, then an undergraduate physics major, took an honors course with Olson titled “Astronomy in Art, History and Literature.” The class changed her life. She partnered with students from other disciplines, she says, using their separate skill sets to find novel solutions to various mysteries. Pope’s first project was to find the dates when one could photograph sunset through a particular V-shaped geological formation in Big Bend National Park in southwest Texas. Olson gave her a puzzle to solve, and she was hooked.

Later in the semester, Olson handed Pope a print of Starry Night —the somewhat more realistic painting by Edvard Munch rather than the more famous one by van Gogh. He asked her to figure out when it was painted. Pope dove into the Munch assignment, calculating astronomical data for the Norwegian resort town of Asgardstrand, where Munch made the painting, a place she’d never visited. Most of the available information about the town’s history was printed in Norwegian, including an archived article from the newspaper Morgenbladet . It confirmed that Munch’s Starry Night had been cataloged in an early exhibition under another name, Abendstern , which, oddly enough, translates to “Evening Star.” Finding this alternate name clarified references to the painting in other historical documents, as well as in Munch’s own hand. It depicted an early evening scene. Importantly, Munch’s bright dot corresponded to the position of Jupiter. Venus was not visible in the sky he painted, and in the 19th century any bright planet after sunset might be called an “evening star.” This narrowed the earliest possible date to July 9, 1893; Munch’s travel records put September 24 as the latest. Weather records further narrowed the date to one of two evenings: August 16 or 23, both of which fit records Pope found for Abendstern .

Impressed, Olson invited Pope to join him; his wife, Marilynn; and others on a research trip to Norway to conduct further investigations into the painting, along with The Storm and other Munch works. She eventually joined ten of Olson’s expeditions, becoming a co-author of six published research papers and appearing in all four of his books . “I created this whole astronomy nerd family,” Pope says of the colleagues she’s met while traveling. “[It’s been] two decades of friendship and research.”

One member of that family is Roger W. Sinnott, a senior editor at Sky & Telescope magazine, where Olson has published many of his results. In 2014, Olson collected some of these articles in Celestial Sleuth: Using Astronomy to Solve Mysteries in Art, History and Literature . More books followed. Celestial Sleuthing: More Mysteries in Art, History and Literature , fourth in the series (which includes a discussion of Friedrich’s The Evening Star ), was published in January 2026.

When approaching a new case, Olson asks four questions about each work examined: Where was the artist located? (Using such tools as computer regressions of lunar, solar and planetary movements combined with angles taken from geologic formations and surviving structures or trees, his group can sometimes determine the artist’s spot within a few feet.) When was the artist there? (Through combined astronomical and historical records, Olson seeks the year, month, day and time, down to the minute if possible.) Which way was the artist looking? (Toward the sky to the north, south, east or west, or toward some direction in between?) What appears in the sky? (For some projects, especially those involving the moon, the object is obvious and may appear in the work’s title, but for others, celestial objects such as comets, meteors or planets are more mysterious.) Searching out evidence such as an artist’s letters and written recollections, other works created in the same vicinity, and period maps, Olson methodically eliminates locations and dates suggested by previous scholars, in the manner of a sharp district attorney destroying a criminal’s alibi.

Of Friedrich’s The Evening Star , he knew that past catalogs had guessed the painting was likely created between 1820 and 1835. Some sources suggested the hill was an invention of the artist, who used it to create an idealized view of Dresden. Olson had read virtually every book on Friedrich, and the uncertainties around this painting, he felt sure, would clear up once he and his team gathered the necessary hard facts.

When Pope wrote to me about the Friedrich painting, she explained that besides helping with astronomical research on the date and location of creation, my photos might corroborate a discovery Olson had made during his investigation of J.M.W. Turner’s Moonlight, a Study at Millbank : Small dots in photographs of paintings were routinely assumed to be dust or image defects and promptly “cleaned up” by photographers—but some of them were probably stars or planets. Perhaps a few unretouched cellphone shots, taken as close as I could get to the actual painting, would clear everything up.

Pope did not have to ask twice. I knew I had to find that dot.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The current iteration of the Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat (FNCB, or the Club) was established in 1952 and continues to thrive, with a healthy and active membership. Since it began, all being well, members have gathered for a monthly Club Meeting and excursion to sites of local natural history interest.

Of the 571 editions of The Ballarat Naturalist available online in the BHL at the time of writing, the December 2025 edition was selected for featuring in this “BHL at 20” Series.

Why? It showcases some of the most celebrated events and people in the Club’s history as events unfolded to bring them together.

Front cover of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dec. 2025 edition. Credit: Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat. View on BHL

There is no prerequisite of any specialist knowledge to join the FNCB, just a desire to learn more about nature and a willingness to be involved in efforts to ensure its preservation. Nevertheless, since its inception, FNCB has been most fortunate to benefit from the vast local knowledge of many notable amateur naturalists who have made exceptional contributions to the Club over many decades.

The most anticipated event on the FNCB’s annual Calendar of Activities is the Stella Bedggood Memorial Lecture. It was inaugurated in 1979 in honour of its late namesake in the year after her premature death to cancer. Mrs Bedggood was an outstanding amateur naturalist, self-taught botanist, conservation advocate, educator and photographer who held various offices in the Club including, most notably, the role of Secretary for 13 years.

Each year, the Lecture features a prominent speaker presenting a talk on a natural history topic relevant to the Ballarat region, often with a conservation thread as befits Mrs Bedggood’s legacy. In 2025, the Lecture was even more special for Club members than usual as it featured Roger Thomas who had just been announced as the winner of the prestigious Australian Natural History Medallion (ANHM) 2025. You can view a video recording of the event here .

The December 2025 edition of The Ballarat Naturalist features the write-up of Mr Thomas’s fascinating presentation titled: “ Ballarat’s Nature Noted: A retrospective of Nature writing over four decades ”. It showcased Mr Thomas’s 41 years of weekly “Nature Notes” articles in The Courier (Ballarat), which chronicled the turning of the seasons, special and unusual observations, threats to species and environments, the lifecycles of local flora and fauna, and trends in their abundance and distribution – a veritable gold mine of local natural history.

These introductions collated information from various sources, including the archive of “Nature Notes” articles penned by Roger Thomas for The Courier , historic editions of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dr Susan Kruss’s PhD thesis, A Voice for Nature: A History of the Field Naturalists Club of Ballarat (2024), and the Club’s nomination of Roger for the ANHM 2025.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Wildwood , set in a magical world in the unruly forests bordering Portland, Oregon, is the newest film from animation house Laika . Founded in 2005, the studio became acclaimed for its work on films such as Coraline (2009) and Kubo and the Two Strings (2016). Laika champions practical effects and stop-motion animation —a flipbook-like filmmaking style in which objects are moved frame by frame to create the action seen on screen. At 2 hours and 12 minutes, Wildwood is the longest stop-motion animated film ever made.

The story follows the courageous Prue and her classmate Curtis as she embarks on a fantasy adventure in the forests to find her kidnapped baby brother. Costume designer Deborah Cook developed more than 200 pieces for Wildwood .

After her work on Tim Burton’s Corpse Bride , Cook was approached by Laika to work on Coraline . “It was a definite yes,” she says of relocating her life from London to Portland to be part of what would become an Oscar-nominated film . After that production, she stuck with the studio. She was interested in how much Laika’s CEO Travis Knight, who directed Wildwood , was invested in stop-motion. “I really wanted to be part of that,” Cook says.

Wildwood is based on the 2011 middle-grade fantasy novel of the same name, written by Colin Meloy and illustrated by Carson Ellis.

In 2019, Cook got the Wildwood project and then the world shut down because of the Covid-19 pandemic the following year. Stuck in Portland, the city where the film would take place, the costume designer found herself exploring the region with a whole new set of eyes. All the while, Cook notes that she was “approaching this movie with a really fantastical element plus contemporary Portland.”

Ahead of Wildwood ’s October 23 release, Cook spoke with Smithsonian magazine about the knits and peacoats that she created to adorn the movie’s characters.

What were your first reactions to hearing the breadth of storytelling for Wildwood and the genres you’d pass through to tell the story in costumes?

It didn’t actually feel too daunting because I feel like it’s a reality that we live in Portland anyway. We work in an animation studio in the actual setting of Wildwood , so we live in that contemporary life in Portland, being aware of what everyone wears. It’s very much an outdoorsy kind of area. But then it’s also full of people with a real high level of imagination and creativity. So it felt like I was partway there to understanding that world already.

It was around 2020, literally the start of lockdown, and this was a fantastic anchor because it almost fit what was happening. I could go out to the end of my road and walk around the Wildwood Trail in Forest Park. That was our “permitted activity” to get outside. I saw so much more in the local nature of my environment than I’d ever really properly absorbed. That was fantastic, and the forest there is magnificent. It really felt quite Jurassic to me. The fact that over Covid, there weren’t as many park keepers meant it became more and more unkempt. Things were growing at a rapid rate and really uncontrollably—you could see that escalation weekly, which was magical in itself.

Walking around in the forest at that time, I was very aware of things that I was looking for to discover the vibe of our characters: Like, what would Prue and Curtis feel when they were walking around the forest? What would be normal to them? What would take them out of that world? What is the first thing you would see that would spark a sort of strange curiosity that there’s something mysterious happening that’s out of the ordinary?

Prue is wearing an everyday town coat to start with. She’s very buttoned up and tucked in. She has a few airs and graces, and she thinks she’s a little older and wiser than she is. But when it comes down to the nitty-gritty of having to go out there and rescue her brother, she switches to something that everyone was wearing at that time going into the forest. It’s a little more casual but practical; very, very pragmatic. Everyone has their clothes that would serve them well in a walk around the forest where any weather or climate might come their way. With her trusty boots and hair tied up, she became more of her true self. It revealed her soul a little more, revealing who she really was in a less guarded moment.

Wildwood takes place in a magical world around Portland. How did you begin to approach that world?

[Prue and Curtis] are going into this forest, and they’re seeing people they don’t recognize. They can’t read them very well. What’s been brought into that world is medieval armor, different ways of making clothing that people might have relied on even if there’d been a parallel civilization that we don’t know about. Where did that clothing come from? Was it left behind by previous civilizations?

There wasn’t anything that got into the impassable wilderness from our world. So it was very much fostering that thought process and understanding what could be in the impassable wilderness but also identifying what each different civilization might be wearing, like what those communities and citizens were wearing that identified them and made them separate from each other.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The MBLWHOI Library’s BHL journey began in 2006 through contributing leadership, technical expertise, and hands-on librarian effort to the exciting BHL start-up period. Today and for many years, a quiet but deliberate process has taken place towards introducing grade school through graduate level students and researchers to the Biodiversity Heritage Library. This happens in a single one-hour-long class students attend in the MBLWHOI Library where BHL is presented as an online tool that students can learn to use to extend their research studies of bound paper science books and journals.

These classes use BHL content to show students (the youngest of whom nowadays have minimal experience using paper books) the look and tactile feel of books that are hundreds of years old, while referencing the BHL digital examples showing the interface of print and online in science publishing, such as bound-in-volume foldouts (foldouts are bound book pages sized larger than the size of the pages of a book and folded into the book). A quick foldout example is shown below, in a plate bound before the first page of volume 8, no. 81 (1672), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London : An attempt of a new kind of telescope invented by Mr. Isaac Newton .

Part of the unique BHL and in-library viewing experience is looking at and being able to download and understand vital details, such as illustrations contained in foldouts. View in BHL .

The Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) was founded in the village of Woods Hole, Massachusetts, in 1888 as America’s first private marine biological laboratory. In 1930, scientists at MBL and the nascent oceanography community collaborated in the founding of another of the key Woods Hole science laboratories, the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI).

In the 1870s, Spencer Fullerton Baird, Secretary of the then recently founded Smithsonian Institution followed through on a charge from US President Ulysses S. Grant to found the US Bureau of Fisheries. Through this process, Baird discovered that the regional waters surrounding the village of Woods Hole are particularly rich in marine biodiversity. This natural phenomenon is influenced by the mixing of warm Gulf Stream currents from the southeast with the cool Labrador currents of the northeast. Secretary Baird also realized that some of the strongest tidal currents on the East Coast of the US are located just off Woods Hole Harbor. See the historical note below from A biological survey of the waters of Woods Hole and vicinity , Sumner, F., Osburn, R., Cole, L. (1911) Bulletin of the Bureau of Fisheries v.31 p.12:

“… Many years ago, Woods Hole was selected by Prof. Baird as the most promising spot upon our coast for the commencement of a scientific study of fisheries problems. From the very outset he gathered about him a staff of naturalists of the type that was dominant in that generation — men eager to seek out every living thing concealed beneath the waves, to describe and figure and name…”

To this day we encourage students to explore the late-summer biodiversity of the waters surrounding Woods Hole by dropping a fishing line to explore the possible diversity of the catch.

On the wall of the office of the MBLWHOI Library is an 1873 poster that was originally hung in the classroom of the Anderson School of Natural History (1873–1875). This poster, with the quote below, was often attributed to Anderson School founder and Harvard professor Louis Agassiz. “Study nature, not books” was a statement reflective of learning through personal experience. The Anderson School of Natural History, which operated on Penikese Island near Woods Hole, was an antecedent of the Marine Biological Laboratory. This school was purposely sited on a postage-stamp-sized island so the students could do their work without summer seaside community distractions. The poster’s statement “Study nature, not books” is appropriate to the MBLWHOI Library and science study in Woods Hole because “learning science by doing science” is how research has traditionally taken place in Woods Hole. We tell the students attending the brief rare books class that we will revisit this quote later in the short class.

1873 poster, “Study nature not books”, from the MBLWHOI Library. Photo courtesy of the author.

In the MBLWHOI Library rare books collection, in Volume 1, number 8 (1666) of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , is an article titled: Directions for sea-men bound for far Voyages . Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London is considered the oldest continuously published scientific journal in the Western world. Its founding in the mid-1660s reflects efforts by scientists and science-interested people in Western Europe and the British Isles to create and document knowledge, compiling references to science experiments and meeting in person or through detailed correspondence to discuss often differing viewpoints on scientific matters. The journal articles which made up Philosophical Transactions were often letters received by the Royal Society, and the proceedings of meetings that took place at the Royal Society in London. Highlighted below are the first few lines of the article, Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages :

“It being the design of the Royal Society, for the better attaining the end of their institution, to study Nature rather than Books , and from the observations, made of the phenomena and effects she presents, to compose such a history of Her, as may hereafter serve to build a solid and useful philosophy upon…to think upon and set down Directions for sea-men going into the East- & West-Indies, the better to capacitate them for making such observations abroad, as may be pertinent and suitable for their purpose…”

Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages , from Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , vol. 1, no. 8, p. 140 (1666). View in BHL .

Students can read on to see that article details are attributed to “Master Rooke”, Lawrence Rooke, a 17th-century English mathematician and astronomer from Gresham College in London. The article goes on to instruct “sea-men bound for far voyages” on what they should be doing to study nature hands-on, meaning: keeping a diary that would include using the instruments of the day to detail the data associated with their voyage: the compass, dipping needles, (another magnetic-field measuring device), visually taking note of the ebbing and flowing of the tides while noting ordinary and extraordinary events, mapmaking, depth measuring, to record and describe weather and astronomical observations, as well as filling and weighing bottles of seawater from different ocean depths.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Since long before the United States was formed, the continent has been the home of Native American people, including the Lakota, Navajo, Sioux, Cherokee, Apache, Dakota and others. The names of those tribes still designate our waterways (the Potomac River, Lake Erie), national parks (Shenandoah and Denali) and even some states (Michigan and Ohio). Native American communities have, of course, contributed more than geographical names and remain a vital part of the fabric of American life. About 7.4 million self-identified Native Americans live in the United States today, and many continue the rich and meaningful traditions of their heritage.

Jeff Campagna is a photo editor at Smithsonian magazine. You can follow him on Instagram at @jeffcampagna .

Tracy Scott Forson is a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine.

items.title: Collections as data: Transcribing the ornithological observations of Walter Faxon
items.author: Joe deVeer
items.summary: Walter Faxon’s ornithological field journals contain thousands of bird observations spanning more than three decades. Now digitized and transcribed using AI-assisted tools, these handwritten records are unlocking historical biodiversity data that could help us better understand environmental change over time.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

With the world facing the dual crisis of climate change and biodiversity loss, the emergence of the Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL) 20 years ago was timely. Over that 20-year span, BHL has grown to become “the world’s largest open access digital library for biodiversity literature and archives” 1 with a corpus of over 64 million pages. This vast corpus is also a repository of historical biodiversity data waiting to be extracted and used to inform a better understanding of anthropogenic effects on climate, the environment, and life on Earth.

Portraits of Walter Faxon taken at graduation from Harvard (1871) and later in life (1896). Harvard College; Heliotype Printing Co.

One “dataset” recently added to BHL is the Ernst Mayr Library ’s (EML) collection of Walter Faxon’s ornithological field journals , field notebooks and bird lists . Faxon (February 4, 1848 – August 10, 1920) was a native of Massachusetts. He was an Assistant Professor of Zoology at Harvard University from 1872 to 1886. Faxon specialized in the study of crustaceans and was Curator of the Invertebrate Department at Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ) for 46 years (1874–1920). He focused his work primarily on the Museum’s collections of Crustacea and Mollusca.

Pencil sketch of Pagurus sp. (hermit crab) first zoeal stage. Drawn by Walter Faxon on 3 August 1881. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.

Ornithology was an avocation for Faxon, but he pursued it with the same level of professionalism with which he approached his curatorial work. He was a Fellow of the American Ornithologists’ Union from 1901–1904. “His long experience in the field [nearly 60 years] and his alertness of eye, ear and mind, as well as his scrupulous care to avoid error, combined to make him one of the best equipped and accurate of field ornithologists – the identification of a bird by him was never questioned.” 2 This inspires confidence in the authenticity of the historical data Faxon left for us, now accessible via the BHL.

The Faxon collection in the Ernst Mayr Library is relatively small, consisting of just over 2,200 pages of manuscript field journals, bird lists, field notebooks, correspondence, eight pencil drawings of Arthropoda and Crustacea, and some additional miscellaneous items. The EML also holds a large collection of William Brewster’s papers that include 145 letters to and from Faxon. Though not voluminous, Faxon’s field journals, bird lists and field notebooks (totaling 1,640 pages) record thousands of bird observations with species name, date, locality, number of individuals seen, and often additional information such as sex, life stage, and vocalization. These species occurrence data, compiled over 33 years (1886–1919), is arguably the greatest asset of Faxon’s collection. Aggregated with similar data from other sources around the world, the resulting dataset will help provide a clear picture of biodiversity change over time, informing efforts to mitigate accelerating species decline.

BHL is well positioned to facilitate development of an aggregated global dataset. By providing the infrastructure and tools to host transcript files for manuscript materials, making the text searchable and scientific names discoverable, BHL promotes extraction of species occurrence data.

With the goal of including Faxon’s data with BHL exports to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), the EML has digitized and transcribed his ornithological observations. In 2025, the collection was digitized with the support of the Harvard Library Collections Digitization Program under the theme of Climate Change. In 2026, the EML was chosen to host a Pforzheimer Fellow to investigate the use of AI-powered tools to transcribe Faxon’s field journals, notebooks, and species lists.

Our Fellow, Mohit Mandal , a Harvard PhD candidate in Anthropology, worked on this project from June 1 to August 31, 2026. He began by evaluating ChatGPT and Google Gemini to determine which model would be best suited for the Faxon materials. Mohit found Gemini to have the edge in accuracy, but more constrained by file upload limits and not as user-friendly, as it works only with Google Workspace tools (e.g., no support for Microsoft Word). He found ChatGPT to be more flexible with follow-up prompting and had success retaining consistency by training the model according to his specifications. Based on this assessment he chose ChatGPT for the project. The initial transcripts were then verified using a different AI tool, Claude, to draw upon the two models’ complementary capabilities and improve overall accuracy.

The screenshots below display page images alongside transcript text in the BHL book viewer. Overall, the results are impressive with pages reviewed thus far revealing relatively few errors. The goal of transcribing nearly 2,000 manuscript pages was achieved. The Pforzheimer Fellowship ended just one week before this writing, so we have not yet had time to calculate an accuracy metric. Some of the difficulties encountered are typical for transcription of handwritten material: notes written in pencil with smudges; marginal text written at an angle (poorly transcribed and, in some instances, not recognized by AI), etc.

One of the greatest challenges was training ChatGPT to capture tiny interlinear numbers and symbols that Faxon would place above the main lines of text (i.e., between lines). This interlinear text would record such things as the number of individual birds of a species seen on a given date, whether the birds were singing, and if they were in a flock. Mohit posits that the difficulty capturing this text may be a consequence of line-spacing constraints with word processors such as Microsoft Word and Google Docs. Ultimately, he was able to preserve the interlinear notations by formatting them as superscript text (Figures 3 and 4).

Left: Extract from Faxon’s April 1890 bird list highlighting his use of interlinear characters. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Thinking. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University. Right: Transcript of the extract with interlinear characters. ChatGPT would often miss these characters, especially on pages with difficult handwriting or on dates appended with more than one character. AI transcription of such characters requires further refinement.

Page 1 of Faxon’s Field Journal, v.1 (1889–91) , with transcript in BHL book viewer. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Pro. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In SAPIENS’ final year of publishing new stories, the magazine honors 10 standout contributions that carried anthropology into the hearts and minds of readers worldwide.

As SAPIENS publishes its final stories, we reflect with gratitude on the remarkable community of anthropologists, journalists, poets, and readers who have made the magazine a home for exploring humanity in all its complexity. In 2025, our contributors wrote about connection and care, loss and return, the voices and conditions that shape us, and the landscapes that hold our histories. More than 3 million readers joined us in this collective journey of understanding. As we close this chapter, the SAPIENS editorial team—Bridget Alex, Amanda Lichtenstein, Ben Schacht, Emily Sekine, Christine Weeber, and myself—offers 10 standout pieces that capture the spirit of what the magazine has always sought to do, illuminate what it means to be human.

—Chip Colwell, Editorial Director

Home-Carrying—A Repatriation Trip to Vanuatu 100 Years in the Making

An anthropologist and poet reflects on a journey of return that tells a larger story about human connection, acts of Indigenous solidarity, and the potential for repair within anthropology.

In a time of heightened threats to reproductive rights, a women’s health scholar and mother of two comes face to face with her uterus.

When Wartime Plunder Comes to Campus

An archaeologist considers whether students should learn from antiquities looted from Iraq.

How Societies Morph With the Seasons

By Cecilia Padilla-Iglesias

An evolutionary anthropologist details seasonal changes among foraging communities—and distills how the fixed political structures of industrialized societies are an outlier in human history.

Why Do Swallows Fly to the Korean DMZ?

An anthropologist discovers diasporic flights—including her own—that begin at and return to the waters of the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.

To Raise Children, We Must First Raise Parents

An anthropologist compares her early motherhood in London with child care experiences in a hunter-gatherer community of Central Africa.

The Day I Heard My Mother’s Accent

In a personal essay, an anthropologist reflects on her family’s dual Syrian and French heritage.

In Human Origins Research, Communities Are the Missing Link

A paleoanthropologist reflects on relationships between researchers and communities living around sites relevant to human evolution.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
An archaeologist studying 1,000-year-old dog burials reflects on the need for imagination in archaeology.

WITH STEADY HANDS, a crouching archaeologist brushes away centuries of soil, revealing the curved edge of a human skull. As they excavate deeper, the slender bones of a dog emerge. The archaeologist pauses, scanning the stillness of this shared grave.

The bones offer the illusion of a story—a villager and his beloved pet, a warrior with her guard dog, or a dog deposited as a spiritual guide in the afterlife. Or perhaps, something this archaeologist has never encountered or read about in their own narrow world.

Archaeologists are tasked with reconstructing the lives and deaths of beings who lived hundreds or thousands of years ago. They search for meaning by examining the arrangement of remains, signs of wear and tear, degraded biomolecules, and other lines of evidence. Even with this arsenal of cutting-edge methods, the past rarely speaks clearly.

When questions about these beings reach into the realm of motivations, beliefs, and identity, what can we know? How much can science say, and when must imagination take over?

As a student using bones and ancient genomes to probe past lives, I’ve been grappling with these questions about the limits of knowledge—especially as I investigate the phenomenon of dogs and humans buried together about 1,000 years ago in Europe’s Baltic region.

As I’ve come to see it, scientists must walk a fine line between silence and sensationalism when they share their conclusions with society. Archaeologists, in particular, should create space for both evidence and imagination, which may open a door to alternate worlds—such as one in which a dog’s meaning transcends your conceptions.

RETHINKING NONHUMAN LIVES

(Non-human) animals in burials are not often considered meaningful in their own right. Even when animals appear in striking burial contexts—dogs curled in graves, mummified cats, horses laid to rest in tombs—their stories are often told secondhand. Usually, the focus is on an animal’s role in human society, with possibilities drawn from archaeologists’ own experiences and worldviews. Wild animals, if recognized at all, are chalked up to ritual or myth. Domesticated horses are seen as transport tools or status symbols. Dogs have often been relegated to the role of servile companion.

Read more from the archives: “The Macabre and Magical Human-Canine Story.”

At best, these conclusions may be uncritical assumptions; at worst, they reinforce “Western” and colonial ontologies that presume other societies share transactional relationships with animals.

One striking example comes from a roughly 1,000-year-old Hopewell mound in what is now Illinois, originally excavated in the 1970s and ’80s. Within the mound, archaeologists unearthed a grave containing an animal skeleton with a string of shell beads around its neck.

Based on its size and shape, the animal was long assumed to be a puppy. The adornment and care shown in its burial led archaeologists to assume the animal was a beloved companion, domesticated and kept by humans. The conclusion made sense from the perspective of many researchers in North America, where people now buy specialty treats and hand-knit sweaters for their pups.

But when the bones were reanalyzed in 2015 by archaeologist Angela Perri and colleagues, they realized the creature was no canine: The grave belonged to a young bobcat.

Burial with intention, with beads and a dedicated grave, doesn’t always signal a domesticated creature—wild animals could also be given elaborate, careful graves.

We researchers today cannot know exactly what the bobcat meant to those who buried it. But we can say the animal meant something. Someone chose to wrap its body, adorn it, and lay it to rest in the ground.

To move beyond conclusions drawn from the world one knows, researchers must look at human-animal relationships more broadly. At Oxford, the Palaeogenomics and Bio-Archaeology Research Network (PalaeoBARN), led by Greger Larson, investigates how animals have moved, bred, and lived alongside humans. One branch of this work, led by researcher AB Siegenthaler, reexamines animal burials that fall outside familiar categories of pets and livestock, considering dogs, snakes, birds, pumas, and cases like the Hopewell bobcat. These burials suggest relationships that resist explanations of utility, ritual, or ownership.

DOGS IN IRON AGE BALTICS

My work with Oxford’s PalaeoBARN, in collaboration with researcher Eduards Plankājs at the University of Latvia, turns a similarly careful eye to roughly 1,000-year-old Iron Age cemeteries where humans and dogs were buried together. In grave after grave of different Iron Age tribes in modern-day Estonia and Latvia, canine skeletons were placed beside human ones, sometimes fully intact, sometimes curled close, sometimes resting at a person’s feet.

To understand the lives behind these burials, our team draws on multiple lines of evidence. We analyze ancient DNA to determine whether the dogs belonged to local lineages or came from elsewhere, tracing patterns of ancestry and migration. We measure chemical isotopes preserved in their bones to answer questions of diet and mobility: Did these animals eat like the people they were buried beside? Did they travel together? And we study their skeletal wear and healing to see how their bodies responded to labor, injury, and age.

Each method offers a window into the experiences of a past creature. Together, these data build a more complete understanding of not just why these dogs were buried with humans, but also how these dogs lived with humans.

Nevertheless, even with all these biological and biomolecular data, there remain many possible narratives produced—or also limited—by archaeologists’ own worldviews or drawn from ethnographic examples. The dogs may have been symbols of status, their bodies placed in the graves of elites with the same intention as a finely worked blade or imported vase. Perhaps the canines were revered as spiritual guardians, buried to protect and guide a community.

Or I might imagine a man and a dog with more closely entangled lives. They shared food and played. The dog slept at the foot of the man’s bed. They grew old together. Upon their deaths, someone made the decision to bury the man and dog as they had lived, side by side.

Whether we imagine status symbols, spiritual guardians, or lifelong companions, each interpretation rests on the same fragments of evidence. Scientific techniques provide archaeologists with increasingly powerful tools for illuminating the past, but there is an often-unrecognized malleability in our interpretations.

It might seem that portraying scientific knowledge as fixed and authoritative would be productive, especially in the current climate of antiscience rhetoric in the U.S., where government agencies are pulling out of the World Health Organization, promoting vaccine skepticism, and denying health care to transgender youth, to name a few examples.

In such a context, it is tempting for researchers to dig our heels in regarding the authority of scientific “truth.” But the misuse of science is not remedied by treating it as unimpeachable.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
SAPIENS’ 2025 poet-in-residence situates her listening in Kashmir and Germany during and after her fieldwork, contextualizing her contributions to SAPIENS this year.

If you missed Uzma Falak’s previous SAPIENS poems, you can find them here.

In the city of
lashed tongues
gashed throats
bleeding ears
LED screens and projectors
wired to sound amplifiers
blare the Minister of Stolen Time’s
Independence Day speech
across empty streets

lashed tongues
gashed throats
bleeding ears
also known as a tourist paradise

In the dispossessed land,
it is the usual scenery:
soldiers guarding empty streets
a labyrinth
of checkpoints
razor wires
steel barricades
perpetually shifting

In the dispossessed land,
it is the usual scenery:
vertigo

Participant Observation

In-flight entertainment screen
shows an Incredible India ad on Kashmir
by the Ministry of Tourism
as I fly from Frankfurt to New Delhi( I arrived in Kashmir in June 2019 for my fieldwork. On August 5, 2019, India unilaterally revoked Article 370 of its Constitution, stripping Kashmir of its nominal autonomy. We woke up to the sound of helicopters, drones, and curfew announcements. Tens of thousands of additional Indian troops were brought into the Valley. Spools of razor wire dotted the streets as new checkpoints and barricades emerged. A communications blackout was imposed marked by the suspension of mobile networks, landlines, internet, satellite television, newspapers, and postal services.)
for my “fieldwork” in Kashmir

Opening scene:
a solitary boat in a serene lake
[slow motion]
[rhythmic sound of oars] [water lapping]
[birdsong] [soft breeze]
[a musical rendition of Habba Khatoon’s poetry] ( Habba Khatoon is a 16th-century poet from Kashmir.)

Last scene:
screen fades to black
an uncanny silence devours sound
as text appears:
Where time stands still

As the flight
from New Delhi lands in Srinagar
we are instructed to
pull down our window shades
on the recommendation of the Ministry of Defence—
current situation, security regulations
so on
and so forth

As the plane shudders on touchdown,
tourists and soldiers on flight
cheer, clap, jump
repeat

Janat e Kashmir—
Paradise of Kashmir,
a large screen glows
above the baggage claim
at Srinagar airport—
a military garrison (Established in 1947 by the Indian Air Force, Srinagar Airport includes a civil enclave administered by the Airports Authority of India.)

Two months later,
the Ministry of Ruins
once again
ransacks our time
seizing its throat
stealing its breath
slashing its heart
until it bleeds to stillness
while the Imperial Clock keeps striking

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
a little pixel dinosaur declares
Unable to connect to the internet
indefinite curfew
lacerated bodies
dead ends
night raids
soundproofing
no signal
crackdown
snap
cut
suspend
repeat

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
silence beaten into a grammar of terror
slashed larynxes
damaged eardrums
on display in glass cabinets
also known as a Museum of Normalcy
PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
dossiers of colonial crimes
tendered as peace treaties

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
Imperial Clock ticking progress
MOVE FORWARD

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
PROVE YOUR IDENTITY
STOP

All characters appearing in this work are fictitious
Any resemblance to real persons, living or dead, is purely coincidental

A voice fills the interrogation room
as the Noise Controller plays a phone audio,
a dream narration:
interrogatee holding two envelopes
one in each hand
standing against the sky
slashed by a
building of mirrored interiors
and echoing hallways
housing the Imperial Clock

Noise Controller
declares the dream to be a covert operation
a coded signal
a prosecutable offence

In the dispossessed land
it is the usual scenery:
Dream Police
off the leash

On a video call home,
I listen to drones
sirens
explosions
resonating through the city’s sternum

Ausländer raus—( This is a German far-right anti-immigrant slogan.)
Foreigners Out
Two teens sing into the night
gliding on a kick scooter
across my street

I listen to roof tiles
crashing to the ground
through an aluminum rubble chute
outside my window
tremoring through my teeth
my body
summoning sounds
shaking my bones,
growing up
inside
the shape of a scream

I listen to police sirens,
emergency announcements
ordering evacuation—
an unexploded World War II bomb
near Heidelberg Central Station
I wander
into the December night
alive with alarms
shattering the regulatory Ruhezeit—(Ruhezeit, German for “quiet time”: legally enforced quiet hours in Germany.)
rising clamor of uncertainty—
home

A voice rises
into the
autumn night wind
in Altstadt
at the student encampment for Palestine
in the university square,
my hands reach for other hands
for the first time in a long, long while

items.cleanReaderHtml:
An archaeologist unspools the story of a female leader buried over 1,000 years ago on the Tibetan Plateau.

A TOMB IN THE HIGHLANDS

In 2005, a truck rumbled down a dirt road in western Tibet, its heavy wheels collapsing ground as it passed. When monks came to clear the debris, they found fragments of a wooden coffin, human bones, and traces of silk.

The accident revealed a tomb beneath the road and a doorway into a forgotten world.

Nearly a decade later, archaeologists returned to excavate the site now known as Gurugyam (གུ་རུ་གྱམ།) Cemetery. Among the many stone-lined burial chambers, one tomb stood out: M2—named using a common convention in Chinese archaeology, where M stands for mu (墓), meaning “tomb,” and the number marks its order of discovery.

The tomb was unusually large and intricately constructed. Whatever precious objects may have once filled it had long disappeared. But the tomb still held scattered bones from what appeared to be a female person—a conclusion later confirmed by ancient DNA analysis.

Who was she? Initially, researchers cast the person in M2 as a sacrificed attendant, assuming a woman would not receive such distinguished burial quarters—an idea more rooted in present-day biases than circumstances of the past. But in the near decade since she surfaced, accumulating evidence suggests the individual was a high-status woman, perhaps a political leader.

And her existence may signal the reality of a place normally described in legends: the “Women’s Kingdom” (女国 Nüguo), written about in 7th- to 8th-century Chinese texts.

I did not meet M2’s occupant in the dust of excavation but on the pages of a research report. As an archaeologist interested in gender and power, I found myself repeatedly returning to her life and her afterlife as the subject of scientific inquiry. I began to glimpse this ancient world where women held power. At the same time, I wondered why her story remains relegated to footnotes of scientific studies, buried in another sense.

TRACES OF A WOMEN’S KINGDOM

Gurugyam Cemetery sits along the upper reaches of the Xiangquan (象泉) River (Langchen Khabub གླང་ཆེན་ཁ་འབབ་) in Tibet’s Ngari (མངའ་རིས།) region. Between 2012 and 2014, archaeologists excavated 11 tombs, eight of which—including the burial known as M2—date to the 3rd and 4th centuries, roughly the end of the Han and Jin period in central China. This was a time of upheaval in the Chinese heartland. The once-mighty Han dynasty collapsed, ushering in an age of warlords and short-lived dynasties, before the Western Jin briefly reunited the realm.

The people who built and used Gurugyam Cemetery lived hundreds of miles west in a Tibetan polity, not under rule by these Chinese dynasties. But the Gurugyam society may have been described by writers living in China’s imperial centers. Ancient texts discuss a far-off “Women’s Kingdom” south of the Pamir Mountains, extending from what is now Tibet’s Ngari (Ali 阿里) region to its borders with Tajikistan and Afghanistan. The Book of Sui (隋书), compiled in the 7th century under the Sui dynasty, records that “south of the Congling Mountains lies a realm ruled by women whose rulers bore the surname Supi … they honor women and belittle men”; the Tongdian (通典), an 8th-century encyclopedic work by Du You (杜佑), offers still more detail: “In that land, women filled official posts, men acted as soldiers; women could have multiple husbands, and children took their mother’s name.”

Whether these were factual observations or imaginative projections, they outlined a strikingly different social order—one that inverted the patriarchal norms of China’s dynasties.

Could Gurugyam, and the female in M2, offer material traces of such a kingdom?

When archaeologists began clearing the cemetery, they uncovered eight tombs sunk into the ground, each a vertical shaft lined with stones. In some they noticed flashes of cinnabar—a vivid red mineral—still clinging to the walls after over 1,000 years. Individuals buried alone were mostly on their sides with bent legs, while the bones in multi-person tombs were found shifted, in disarray.

Graves held finely woven silk, bronze vessels, ceramics, wooden objects, and iron tools. Golden funerary masks and a brocade bearing the characters for “noble” (王侯),  hint at the elevated social status for some of the dead. Archaeologists also found barley grains—some alongside remnants of woven bags that once held them—and bones from cattle, sheep, and horses. Perhaps the foods were offerings or part of some other funerary ritual.

The remains within M2 belonged to a female, estimated to be between 25 and 30 years old. Though not unusually large, her tomb was meticulously constructed from three distinct types of stone. Its floor was hardened by fire, and the walls were coated in cinnabar. In addition to the human remains, the tomb also contained two complete horse skeletons, one complete sheep, and a scatter of other animal bones.

In excavation layers above M2, archaeologists found a pit packed with sheep bones—placement that suggests people came with offerings to remember or venerate the deceased after her death.

Although M2’s lavish design seems to confirm its occupant’s importance, her elite status was not immediately clear. By the time the archaeologists excavated M2 in 2014, its female skeleton was broken and incomplete. Though looting in the modern era probably caused the damage, some archaeologists saw the scene and had other thoughts: They wondered whether she was not the tomb’s master but a sacrificed attendant.

Yet multiple lines of evidence contradict this view.

RECONSTRUCTING A LIFE

Archaeologists working at Gurugyam noted that M2’s vault was the largest and most elaborate tomb. Ancient DNA analyses reported in 2020 revealed the person inside shared close kinship ties with other individuals buried at Gurugyam, confirming the place as a family cemetery.

The timing and location of her burial seem to fit the region and era described in Chinese chronicles of a Women’s Kingdom. The earliest clear written reference to a “Women’s Kingdom” appears in the mid-5th century, when it was listed among exotic goods exchanged in diplomatic contacts.

The chronicles speak of salt-rich valleys where caravans wound their way across the mountains through the Women’s Kingdom. Perhaps a depiction of these salt traders, rock art on the plateau shows lines of figures stooped under heavy loads. The salt routes overlapped with Silk Road branches, encounters that would have brought silk, tea, and other goods into the highlands.

Foods from afar likely fed the M2 individual, based on analyses on chemical signatures embedded in her bones. A 2023 study of stable isotopes—atoms of the same element that differ in weight—revealed her bones harbored an unusually high ratio for carbon and low ratio for nitrogen. This combination points to a diet rich in plants like millet and sorghum—crops that do not thrive at high altitudes—and suggests her food likely arrived through long-distance trade. Compared with others buried nearby, her meals were more varied and higher quality, a testament to her elevated social status.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
An anthropologist traces how transgender women navigate state-sponsored religious programs aimed at “rehabilitating” LGBTQ+ Muslims.

Dora and I walked through the quiet nighttime streets of Chow Kit, a downtown neighborhood in Kuala Lumpur. (All names have been changed to protect people’s privacy. ) Pungent food smells mingled with the sweet scent of fruit and flowers from a nearby market. Abandoned rainbow-colored confetti shivering under the dim, yellowish streetlights reminded us of some celebration that took place earlier. (The author’s research was carried out within the Emmy Noether Junior Research Group “The Bureaucratization of Islam and Its Socio-Legal Dimensions in Southeast Asia,” funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) from 2016 to 2023. The writing of this essay was supported by the FERBOPO Research Project (Grant Agreement ID: 101184092).)

In the 1970s and 1980s, Chow Kit was a bustling red-light district. Today only around 15 to 20 sex workers can be seen on any given night, according to Dora. The decline is due to a worsening economy and increased surveillance by Islamic authorities.

“Most hide from the religious police in these rundown buildings, hoping to find clients using apps,” she said. As we passed a police station, Dora explained that officers required bribes from each sex worker to allow them to work. A local mafioso further exploited them, demanding “protection money” while offering no real security.

Many of the sex workers are transgender women who moved to the city from rural areas at a young age to begin their transitioning journey. But employers in Malaysia often discriminate against trans people, leaving sex work as the only means of survival for some.

Dora was one of many trans women I met while living in Malaysia in 2018 to conduct anthropological fieldwork with the trans community and with Islamic authorities. Dora had never engaged in sex work, but as a trans woman and advocate, she was intimately familiar with the challenges faced by most of her trans “sisters.” While we sat at a streetside food stall and sipped on sweet teh tarik (hot milk tea), Dora reflected, “When you are in Chow Kit, you are nobody. That’s how people see you.”

In recent decades, Malaysia’s state and religious institutions, which jointly govern following conservative Islamic interpretations, have heavily invested in the “moral reform” of citizens labeled deviant. Trans people are criminalized under both sharia and civil law. Trans women can be arrested for “posing as woman” and subjected to jail, fines, or religious “counseling.” They are denied basic rights, excluded from certain jobs, and often humiliated or abused for their identities.

Starting in 2011, the central government’s Department of Islamic Development (JAKIM), which oversees the implementation of sharia law, has launched programs to “guide” LGBTQ+ Malay Muslims “back to the right path” (kembali ke pangkal jalan in Malay). Working with local state religious councils, universities, and Islamic non-governmental organizations, JAKIM issues training manuals, holds talks, and funds research promoting the idea that LGBTQ+ people can be “cured” through religious rehabilitation. It also organizes Mukhayyam, or Islamic camps, to “rehabilitate” transgender individuals. The trans women I met who had attended these rehabilitation camps and programs understood their true purpose: to convince them that living as trans was sinful.

During my fieldwork, I met trans people from all walks of life: activists, NGO workers, sex workers, beauticians, artists, hospitality workers, and corporate employees. Some struggled against state-imposed interpretations of Islam, which do not accept trans people. But many found a supportive community in Kuala Lumpur and embraced their lives as Muslim women. Their paths to self-acceptance were diverse and are ongoing.

Many of the trans women I met in Kuala Lumpur shared they had felt a mismatch since childhood between their male bodies and female identities. Some trans women activists now in their late 40s or early 50s, such as Dora, first met through the PT Foundation, a pioneering organization founded in 1987 to support the LGBTQ+ community during the HIV/AIDS crisis. As global discourses on human rights and gender identity reached the region around the early 2000s, more transgender people in Malaysia began to “come out”—with a new language for articulating what they had long felt. The identity term “mak nyah,” coined by the community in the 1980s, has now been largely replaced in activist and policy circles with “trans women” (or trans wanita, a hybrid English-Malay term).

However, increased visibility and access to information have not led to greater legal protection or societal acceptance. Instead, conservative voices in Malaysia and neighboring countries have grown louder in advocating for the “correction” of trans individuals. Under this political climate, Mukhayyam camps and similar programs proliferated.

Held regularly at tourist locations to attract attendees, the Mukhayyam have strict daily schedules, including prayers, religious classes, health talks, and physical activities like jungle trekking intended to enhance “masculine features” among trans women. While publicly framed as vocational training and public health programs, these camps are based on unfounded, fabricated, and harmful claims, including stereotypes that most trans women are sex workers with HIV/AIDS who need saving.

Read more from the SAPIENS archives: “Stop Erasing Transgender Stories from History.”

Contrary to official claims about the success of Islamic “rehabilitation” for trans people, I never heard any trans women say the programs “corrected” their gender identity.

Some trans women I met who participated in a program similar to Mukhayyam, established by one of the State Islamic Religious Councils, joined seeking community, a weekend trip, or deeper Islamic understanding. But most were older, ill, or in need of zakat, the Islamic financial assistance the program offered. Typically, zakat is meant for all Muslims in need without any obligation in return, but trans participants can only receive this aid money—usually enough to cover monthly rent and food expenses—if they contractually commit to attending the program.

Malaysian state-sponsored authorities and their supporters deny their practices share similarities with other “conversion therapy” practices that claim to “cure” queer and trans people. These can involve exorcism, medication, confinement, electroshock therapy, behavioral conditioning, and verbal, physical, and sexual abuse. In 2020, JAKIM reported an LGBTQ+ activist to the police simply for comparing the rehabilitation camps to “Western” conversion therapy. However, several Malaysian NGOs and LGBTQ+ rights groups have spoken out against Mukhayyam and similar programs, presenting evidence that they do use violent, coercive techniques associated with other conversion therapies found globally.

Over the past several decades, human rights organizations such as Amnesty International and academic societies such as the American Psychological Association have denounced conversion therapy practices aimed at LGBTQ+ people as harmful and “amounting to torture” in some cases. While these practices are banned in some countries, such programs continue to receive support from national policy initiatives and religious organizations. Conversion therapy programs remain legal in most parts of the world and are on the rise again in increasingly conservative and authoritarian states, including in the United States.

NAVIGATING LIFE AS MALAY MUSLIM WOMEN

I met Ana, a devout Muslim and Dora’s acquaintance, in one of the state-sponsored “rehabilitation” programs. She initially joined for financial help and religious learning, but had grown disillusioned. Still, Ana remained in the program on and off for years, partly to receive zakat and partly to challenge the program’s agenda. She resisted the religious teacher’s efforts to make her conform to male rituals and appearances, and regularly challenged the anti-trans rhetoric of the program.

Some of Ana’s peers in the program compromised and changed their physical appearance to resemble a male person, although they claimed they were still women inside. JAKIM showcases these “repented” trans women as success stories. “Some don’t know who they are,” Ana told me.

I met other trans women who struggled more to find the self-acceptance Ana achieved. For example, I spoke with Zita, who was homeless and earned a living through sex work.

“How did it feel when you came out?” I asked.

“I felt relieved, like I didn’t have to pretend anymore,” she said. “But in the end, I’m still pretending.”

I could not hide my surprise. “Are you pretending?”

She sat quietly for a while before answering my question. “Yeah, in a way. I am pretending to God. Yes. Pretending to myself. Yes. That is hypocrisy,” Zita said in a shaky voice.

She believed that being trans was sinful, which is what most religious leaders preached. “Of course, this [being trans] is wrong. But what are we supposed to do? How are people like me supposed to survive? I cannot live like a man, that’s also hypocrisy,” Zita said.

Contrary to official claims, I never heard any trans women say the programs “corrected” their gender identity.
